title: cloud-controller-manager accepts the NativeHistograms feature gate but never applies it
body:
### What happened?

`NativeHistograms` (KEP-5808) is Beta and enabled by default since v1.37. Each component must call
`metricsfeatures.ApplyFeatureGates()` for histograms to pick up the gate state:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/6c1c7702cf2052245ef10e699d45f071af306f59/staging/src/k8s.io/component-base/metrics/features/kube_features.go#L51-L56

This is done in kube-apiserver, kube-scheduler, kube-controller-manager, kube-proxy and kubelet,
the five components listed in KEP-5808.

However, `k8s.io/cloud-provider/app` also registers the metrics feature gates, so
cloud-controller-manager accepts `--feature-gates=NativeHistograms=true` and
`DefaultFeatureGate.Enabled(NativeHistograms)` returns true, but nothing calls
`ApplyFeatureGates`:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/6c1c7702cf2052245ef10e699d45f071af306f59/staging/src/k8s.io/cloud-provider/app/controllermanager.go#L68-L71

So on every cloud-controller-manager built on `k8s.io/cloud-provider/app`, the gate reports as
enabled (by default since v1.37) but has no effect, and histograms stay classic-only.
The same is true in v1.37.0.

### What did you expect to happen?

Either cloud-controller-manager histograms are exposed in both classic and native formats when
`NativeHistograms` is enabled, like the other control-plane components, or, if
cloud-controller-manager is intentionally out of scope, the gate should not silently appear
enabled there with no effect.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

No cluster is needed. This test drives the real `NewCloudControllerManagerCommand` and checks,
from the `cloudInitializer` hook (which runs after `Config()`), whether a newly created
histogram is native:

<details>
<summary>Test snippet</summary>

```go
cloudInitializer := func(*config.CompletedConfig) cloudprovider.Interface {
	gateEnabled := utilfeature.DefaultFeatureGate.Enabled(metricsfeatures.NativeHistograms)
	nativeBefore := histogramIsNative(t, "repro_before_seconds") // NewHistogram + Gather, checks Schema != nil
	metricsfeatures.ApplyFeatureGates(utilfeature.DefaultFeatureGate)
	nativeAfter := histogramIsNative(t, "repro_after_seconds")
	// ...
}
cmd := app.NewCloudControllerManagerCommand(s, cloudInitializer, app.DefaultInitFuncConstructors,
	names.CCMControllerAliases(), cliflag.NamedFlagSets{}, stopCh)
cmd.SetArgs([]string{"--kubeconfig=<dummy>", "--cloud-provider=fake",
	"--feature-gates=NativeHistograms=true", "--secure-port=0", "--webhook-secure-port=0"})
```

</details>

Output at master (6c1c7702cf2):

```
NativeHistograms gate enabled in CCM:                true
histogram native after CCM startup (Config done):   false
histogram native after calling ApplyFeatureGates:    true
```

I'm happy to share the full test.

### Anything else we need to know?

I noticed that KEP-5808 lists only five components, so I'm not sure whether leaving out
cloud-controller-manager was a deliberate scoping decision. Either way, the gate currently
looks enabled but silently does nothing there, which seems worth resolving in one of two ways:

1. Wire it up: call `features.ApplyFeatureGates(utilfeature.DefaultFeatureGate)` in the
   cloud-controller-manager `RunE`, right after `logsapi.ValidateAndApply`. That is before
   `s.Config()` builds REST clients and informers, so it also avoids the ordering problem
   described in #142379. A cloud-controller-manager case could be added to
   `test/integration/metrics/nativehistograms/metrics_test.go`.
2. If cloud-controller-manager is intentionally out of scope, make that explicit, for example
   in the KEP or the feature-gate docs, so cloud-provider maintainers aren't surprised.

Happy to send a PR for option 1 if that's the preferred direction.

Related: #128842, #142379, #142377.

AI tools assisted with the investigation; I reviewed the code and ran the reproduction myself.

/sig cloud-provider
/sig instrumentation

### Kubernetes version

<details>

Reproduced from source at master 6c1c7702cf2052245ef10e699d45f071af306f59 (v1.38 development).
Confirmed the same code is in v1.37.0 (`ApplyFeatureGates` is not called in `k8s.io/cloud-provider/app`).

</details>

### Cloud provider

<details>
Any cloud-controller-manager built on `k8s.io/cloud-provider/app`. Reproduced with a unit test, so no cloud is involved.
</details>

### OS version

Windows 11 (build 26200), go1.27.1. Not OS-specific.

### Install tools

<details>
N/A, reproduced from source
</details>


### Container runtime (CRI) and version (if applicable)

<details>
N/A
</details>


### Related plugins (CNI, CSI, ...) and versions (if applicable)

<details>
N/A
</details>

title: [Declarative Validation] Track beta→stable graduation of validation rules
body:
### What would you like to be added?

A tracking issue for the beta→stable graduation of declarative validation rules, per KEP-5073.

Every DV rule currently at beta carries `since: "1.37"`, and there are no older ones, so nothing was eligible until v1.37 shipped. It has, which opens the wave.

### Scope

Settled in [this comment](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/141532#issuecomment-5403123232):

- **One API type per PR**, not one group. The type is the kind: a nested struct such as `IPBlock` goes with `NetworkPolicy`, not in a PR of its own. Deleting handwritten validation has no per-rule rollback and costs the mismatch comparison its baseline, so diffs stay small enough to read line by line.
- **`+k8s:beta` to stable only.** Dropping the prefix. `+k8s:alpha` promotion is out of scope and handled separately.
- **`meta` / ObjectMeta is out of scope** and tracked separately. This catches whole rows: `lifecycle`'s two rules are both on the embedded `metav1.ObjectMeta` (`lifecycle/v1alpha1/types.go:59` and `:251`), so that group is not claimable here.

The group rows below size the backlog. The unit of work, and of claiming, is a single API type inside one of them.

### Backlog

Regenerated at `451ab1d9b7c`:

| API group | beta rules | Status | Owner | PR |
|---|---:|---|---|---|
| `resource` | 410 | unclaimed | | |
| `flowcontrol` | 40 | unclaimed | | |
| `rbac` | 21 | in review | @itzPranshul | #141605 |
| `networking` | 20 | partly claimed | @liyuerich | NetworkPolicy (6). `IngressClass` (6) and `IPAddress` (8) unclaimed |
| `storage` | 12 | in review | @itzPranshul | #142056 (VolumeAttachment). #141967 (StorageClass) merged 2026-09-15 |
| `certificates` | 12 | in review | @antcybersec | #142333 (CertificateSigningRequest) |
| `autoscaling` | 12 | in review | @datayurei | #142151 (HorizontalPodAutoscaler, 10). The other 2 are `Scale`, see `apps` |
| `extensions` | 8 | **not workable** | | no `pkg/apis/extensions/validation/` exists, so there is nothing to delete; `extensions/v1beta1` is the one entry in `coverage-allowlist.yaml`, "Not served by kube-apiserver" |
| `admissionregistration` | 6 | in review | @alinaqvi1129 | #142222 (ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding) |
| `apps` | 4 | unclaimed | | all four are `ScaleSpec.replicas` in `v1beta1`/`v1beta2`. They graduate together with `autoscaling/v1` `Scale` as one PR: 6 rules, one handwritten check in `ValidateScale` |
| `core` | 2 | **out of scope** | @yongruilin | #141564 (ReplicationControllerSpec, merged). The remaining 2 are on ReplicationController's `metav1.ObjectMeta` |
| `lifecycle` | 2 | **out of scope** | | both rules are on `metav1.ObjectMeta`, see Scope |
| `node` | 0 | done | @krishhna24 | #142119 (RuntimeClass, merged 2026-09-16) |
| `discovery` | 0 | done | @krishhna24 | #141533 (EndpointSlice, merged 2026-09-03) |
| `batch` | 0 | done | @alinaqvi1129 | #141677 (CronJob, merged 2026-09-14) |
| **total** | **549** | | | |

`authorization`, `scheduling`, `policy` and `storagemigration` carry alpha rules only, so they have nothing to graduate here.

Counts move as the wave lands. The total was 592 at filing, then 588, then 574 after #141533 (`discovery`) and #141677 (`batch`), and is 549 now: #141967 took `storage` 28 to 12 and #142119 took `node` 9 to 0. Only `types.go` carries the markers, so this returns the same number:

```
grep -rho --include='*.go' '+k8s:beta(since:' staging/src/k8s.io/api | wc -l
```

### Claiming

Comment here naming the **API type** you are taking, then open one PR for it. I will keep the table current.

On sourcing Owner from the tag's `owner:` field: that field does not exist. `+k8s:alpha` and `+k8s:beta` accept at most one argument and it has to be `since`, matching a version regex, so anything else is a generator error (`staging/src/k8s.io/code-generator/cmd/validation-gen/validators/levels.go:64-74`). A `grep -rho 'owner:' staging/src/k8s.io/api` returns nothing. So Owner comes from claims in this thread instead, unless you would rather the tag grew the field.

### Why is this needed?

The KEP's criteria for beta→stable are ">=1 release at Beta, zero mismatch/panic metrics, reviewers agree the safety switch is no longer needed", and "the same PR removes the matching handwritten validation".

The first two are checkable in-tree. `pkg/api/testing/validation.go` already asserts `apiserver_validation_declarative_validation_mismatch_total == 0` under both gate configurations, so a graduation can be verified locally rather than from production dashboards.

The third is a reviewer judgement, which is why this is an issue and not just a series of PRs.

### Worth writing down

Dropping the wrapper and deleting the handwritten check are **not** separable. `FilterCoveredHandwrittenErrors` only suppresses a handwritten error when a matching *beta* declarative error is enforced, so a graduated rule that still has its handwritten twin reports the same violation twice and trips the mismatch metric. Demonstrated in #141533.

/sig api-machinery
/area api-validation
/kind cleanup

title: Was leaving NativeHistogramMinResetDuration unset in component-base intentional?
body:
First of all, thank you for landing native histogram support in v1.37 — it's been a really
welcome addition on my side. In my own testing on a kind cluster, scraping the control plane
metrics as native-only cut the number of stored series by roughly 75%, and no longer being
bounded by the classic bucket boundaries has already changed how I'm approaching SLI design.

While evaluating it, I ran into something I wasn't sure how to read. Apologies in advance if
this has already been discussed somewhere I've missed.

`component-base` sets two of the native histogram options:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.37.0/staging/src/k8s.io/component-base/metrics/internal/nativehistograms.go#L33-L40

```go
var defaultNativeHistogramOptions = NativeHistogramOptions{
	BucketFactor:    1.1,
	MaxBucketNumber: 160,
}
```

`NativeHistogramMinResetDuration` is left at zero. As far as I can tell, that means once a
histogram exceeds `MaxBucketNumber`, `maybeReset()` is skipped and only `doubleBucketWidth()`
runs, so the reduced resolution stays in place for the lifetime of the process:

https://github.com/prometheus/client_golang/blob/v1.24.0/prometheus/histogram.go#L478-L480

```go
//  - Any increased zero threshold or reduced resolution is reset back
//    to their original values once NativeHistogramMinResetDuration has
//    passed (since the last reset or the creation of the histogram).
```

A few other projects in the ecosystem do set it to `1h`:

| repo | org | BucketFactor | MaxBucketNumber | MinResetDuration |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| controller-runtime | kubernetes-sigs | 1.1 | 100 | `1h` |
| cluster-api | kubernetes-sigs | 1.1 | 100 | `1h` |
| Prometheus | prometheus | 1.1 | 100 | `1h` |

That said, I can imagine a reason not to: `maybeReset()` also clears `_sum`, `_count` and the
classic buckets, which may well be something you'd want to avoid for `STABLE` metrics.
KEP-5808 explains the reasoning behind `BucketFactor` and `MaxBucketNumber` but doesn't touch
on reset behaviour, so I couldn't tell whether this was weighed and set aside, or simply
hasn't come up yet.

Could you help me understand which it is? I'd be glad to open a PR if it turns out to be just
an oversight, though I wanted to ask first in case there's context I'm missing.

/sig instrumentation
/kind bug

title: Idle watchers in kube-apiserver significantly degrade write throughput, watch latency, and memory
body:
Idle watchers in kube-apiserver have a large cost on write throughput, watch propagation latency, internal watcher stability, CPU, and memory even when they receive zero events and add zero allocations.

We added a write-throughput benchmark with 50,000 idle ConfigMap watches ([kubernetes/test-infra#38010](https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/pull/38010)) alongside the 2,000 QPS Pod patch benchmark (`n2-standard-32` control plane, 10,000 Pods, 0 external Pod watchers):

| Metric | [0 Idle Watchers](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/pr-logs/pull/142887/pull-kubernetes-benchmark-write-throughput/2108639959085748224) | [50k Idle Watchers](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-benchmark-write-throughput-idle-watchers/2108635522078347264) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 200-OK Pod Patch Throughput ([PerfDash](https://perf-dash.k8s.io/#/?jobname=benchmark%20write%20throughput%20idle%20watchers&metriccategoryname=GenericMeasurements&metricname=SuccessfullyHandledPatchRequests&code=200&resource=pods&verb=PATCH)) | 2,000 req/s (0% HTTP 429s) | 1,801 req/s (10% HTTP 429s) |
| Pod Patch Latency (P50 / P90 / P99, [PerfDash](https://perf-dash.k8s.io/#/?jobname=benchmark%20write%20throughput%20idle%20watchers&metriccategoryname=GenericMeasurements&metricname=APIServerPatchLatency&resource=pods&verb=PATCH)) | 34 / 135 / 317 ms (0 > 1s) | 121 / 371 / 683 ms (2,785 > 1s, fails 1s SLO) |
| Pod Watch Queue Latency (P50 / P99, [PerfDash](https://perf-dash.k8s.io/#/?jobname=benchmark%20write%20throughput%20idle%20watchers&metriccategoryname=GenericMeasurements&metricname=WatchEventsDispatchLatency&resource=pods&stage=watcher_queue_latency)) | 5.9 / 31.1 ms | 414 / 4,851 ms (70x / 156x) |
| Storage-to-WatchCache Latency (P50 / P99, [PerfDash](https://perf-dash.k8s.io/#/?jobname=benchmark%20write%20throughput%20idle%20watchers&metriccategoryname=GenericMeasurements&metricname=WatchEventsDispatchLatency&resource=pods&stage=storage_to_cache)) | 26.7 / 40.7 ms | 82.0 / 1,266 ms (3.1x / 31x) |
| WatchCache Read Wait (Avg / P99, [PerfDash](https://perf-dash.k8s.io/#/?jobname=benchmark%20write%20throughput%20idle%20watchers&metriccategoryname=GenericMeasurements&metricname=WatchCacheReadWaitLatency&resource=pods)) | 68.8 / 199 ms | 590 / 2,988 ms (8.6x / 15x) |
| Internal Pod Watch Terminations ([PerfDash](https://perf-dash.k8s.io/#/?jobname=benchmark%20write%20throughput%20idle%20watchers&metriccategoryname=GenericMeasurements&metricname=WatchTerminationRate&resource=pods)) | 3 | 227 |
| KCM Pod Informer Lag (P90 / P99, [PerfDash](https://perf-dash.k8s.io/#/?jobname=benchmark%20write%20throughput%20idle%20watchers&metriccategoryname=GenericMeasurements&metricname=InformerCacheLagPrometheus&name=kube-controller-manager)) | 1.3 / 1.4 s | 47.1 / 86.3 s (62x P99) |
| Scheduler Pod Informer Lag (P90 / P99, [PerfDash](https://perf-dash.k8s.io/#/?jobname=benchmark%20write%20throughput%20idle%20watchers&metriccategoryname=GenericMeasurements&metricname=InformerCacheLagPrometheus&name=kube-scheduler)) | 2.0 / 2.1 s | 12.5 / 63.4 s (29x P99) |
| Storage Update Conflicts (P50 / P99, [PerfDash](https://perf-dash.k8s.io/#/?jobname=benchmark%20write%20throughput%20idle%20watchers&metriccategoryname=GenericMeasurements&metricname=StorageUpdateConflictRate&operation=update&resource=pods)) | 14.2 / 24.7 /s | 37.9 / 544.6 /s (2.7x / 22x) |
| Go Scheduler Latency (P50 / P99, [PerfDash](https://perf-dash.k8s.io/#/?jobname=benchmark%20write%20throughput%20idle%20watchers&metriccategoryname=GenericMeasurements&metricname=GoSchedLatency&endpoint=apiserver)) | 4.8 / 6.3 ms | 49.9 / 84.5 ms (10.5x / 13.5x) |
| apiserver CPU (P50 / P99, [PerfDash](https://perf-dash.k8s.io/#/?jobname=benchmark%20write%20throughput%20idle%20watchers&metriccategoryname=GenericMeasurements&metricname=ContainerCPU&container=kube-apiserver)) | 20.4 / 21.3 cores | 24.7 / 26.1 cores |
| apiserver Memory (P50 / P99, [PerfDash](https://perf-dash.k8s.io/#/?jobname=benchmark%20write%20throughput%20idle%20watchers&metriccategoryname=GenericMeasurements&metricname=ContainerMemory&container=kube-apiserver)) | 10.4 / 10.8 GB | 20.3 / 21.3 GB |

title: [Flaking Test] [sig-scheduling] TestCPGScheduling: PodGroup/CompositePodGroup "Scheduled" condition sometimes never set (test/integration/scheduler podgroup)
body:
### Which jobs are flaking?

- ci-kubernetes-integration-master ([sig-release-master-blocking](https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-release-master-blocking#integration-master))
- ci-kubernetes-integration-master-s390x

### Which tests are flaking?

`[sig-scheduling] k8s.io/kubernetes/test/integration/scheduler podgroup`

- `TestCPGScheduling/TestCPGBasicWithGangChildren`
- `TestCPGScheduling/TestCPGMinGroupCount`


### Since when has it been flaking?

2026-09-28. The first failure was the same day #140670 merged, which added these tests. Triage showed 11 failures between 2026-09-28 and 2026-10-04 (9 on s390x, 2 on amd64), and it failed again on amd64 in the build above on 2026-10-05.

### Testgrid link

https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-release-master-blocking#integration-master

### Reason for failure (if possible)

[Triage](https://storage.googleapis.com/k8s-triage/index.html?job=ci-kubernetes-integration-master&test=%20k8s.io%2Fkubernetes%2Ftest%2Fintegration%2Fscheduler)
[Prow](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-integration-master/2107038346378219520)

Failing with:
```
Failed
=== RUN   TestCPGScheduling/TestCPGMinGroupCount
    stepsframework.go:794: Executing step step 0 name Create Node
    stepsframework.go:794: Executing step step 1 name Create Workload
    stepsframework.go:794: Executing step step 2 name Create root CPG
    stepsframework.go:794: Executing step step 3 name Create pg1
    stepsframework.go:794: Executing step step 4 name Create pg2
    stepsframework.go:794: Executing step step 5 name Create pg3
    stepsframework.go:794: Executing step step 6 name Create Pods
    stepsframework.go:794: Executing step step 7 name Wait for successful pods
    stepsframework.go:794: Executing step step 8 name Verify failing pods remain unschedulable
    stepsframework.go:794: Executing step step 9 name Verify root CPG and pg1, pg2 conditions are Scheduled
    cpg_test.go:932: Test failed: step 9 (Verify root CPG and pg1, pg2 conditions are Scheduled) failed: failed to wait for CompositePodGroup cpg-root condition (status=True, reason=Scheduled): context deadline exceeded
--- FAIL: TestCPGScheduling/TestCPGMinGroupCount (34.58s)

=== RUN   TestCPGScheduling
--- FAIL: TestCPGScheduling (81.88s)
```

### Anything else we need to know?

The pods schedule as expected (the "Wait for successful pods" and "Verify failing pods remain unschedulable" steps pass), but the `Scheduled` condition is never set on the root CompositePodGroup or on one of its child PodGroups. The wait then times out after `wait.ForeverTestTimeout` (30s).

Two variants seen:

```
cpg_test.go:932: Test failed: step 9 (Verify root CPG and pg1, pg2 conditions are Scheduled) failed: failed to wait for CompositePodGroup cpg-root condition (status=True, reason=Scheduled): context deadline exceeded
```
```
cpg_test.go:932: Test failed: step 8 (Verify root CPG and pg1 conditions are Scheduled) failed: failed to wait for PodGroup pg1 condition (status=True, reason=Scheduled): context deadline exceeded
```

Timeline from the example build (`TestCPGBasicWithGangChildren`, UTC):

- 09:45:08.79 - 08.81: pods created; the scheduler processes `cpg-root`
- ~09:45:09.6: `waitForGroupsScheduled` starts. It checks CPGs first, then PodGroups. `cpg-root` passes on the first poll, so its condition was already set.
- 09:45:09.6 - 39.4: `pg1` is polled every 100ms for 30s and never gets `Scheduled=True`. No scheduler log output appears in this window.
- 09:45:39.6: timeout

This doesn't look like a slow-machine timeout. The whole scheduling cycle completes in well under a second, and the parent's status is written quickly. The child's status update, from the same scheduling decision, never lands. That suggests the status update for one group in the hierarchy is occasionally dropped or skipped, rather than delayed. It reproduces on amd64 as well as s390x.

### Relevant SIG(s)

/sig scheduling

title: Migrate 'Good First Migration' Immutable Fields to Declarative Validation
body:
### What would you like to be added?

This issue tracks a number of identified "good first migration" cases from handwritten Go code to Declarative Validation tags (`+k8s:immutable` or `+k8s:update=NoModify`) as part of KEP-5073. This issue aims to be a more narrowed down list with specific fields and validation tags than the general tracking issues. The goal is to have users more easily able to aid in the migration by first having a set of "Good First Migration" cases with minimal migration friction and build from there.

For more information on the tasks here, the Declarative Validation work group (guiding this and similar issues) has open discussion in kubernetes Slack channel: `#sig-api-machinery-dev-tools`

We are targeting fields that meet the "Good First Migration" criteria:
1.  **Validation Logic:** Simple immutability checks (typically using `apivalidation.ValidateImmutableField` or direct equality checks between `new` and `old` objects).
2.  **Versioning:** The field exists at the same path across all API versions.
3.  **Status:** The field has not yet been migrated (does not currently have a `+k8s:immutable` or `+k8s:update` tag).

### IMPORTANT! - PR Structure
The ideal PR structure for a PR contributing a DV tag migration is:

*   **Commit # 1:** IF NOT ALREADY WIRED UP FOR DV - Wire up the apigroup, add empty test and empty generated file.
*   **Commit # 2:** Use a single DV tag on a single field. E.g. Add `+k8s:immutable` to an immutable field. Includes generated code and robust test cases. Emphasis on test-cases -- we want enough to prove that a field is correct, but we don't want to duplicate all the per-tag tests.
*   **Commits # 3...N:** Use DV tags on the same field, one per commit; repeat until that field is done or all that is left is not handled by DV yet.
*   **Commits N+1...M:** Repeat the above for more fields.

The emphasis is on lots of small commits. Maintaining commit discipline is hard but worthwhile.

### Resources

*   **KEP:** [KEP-5073: Declarative Validation](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-api-machinery/5073-declarative-validation)
*   **Migration Guide:** [Review the "Migrating Handwritten Validation" section in the README](https://github.com/jpbetz/validation-gen/blob/main/staging/src/k8s.io/code-generator/cmd/validation-gen/README.md#2-migrating-handwritten-validation-to-declarative-validation)

### Understanding `+k8s:update` Options

When migrating immutable fields, you will primarily use `+k8s:immutable` or `+k8s:update=NoModify`. Here is when to use which:

*   **`+k8s:immutable`**: Use this for fields that, once set (during creation or update), can never be changed. It is the most common tag for "immutable" fields. It is equivalent to `+k8s:update=NoModify` but conveys the intent of "immutability" more clearly for the entire lifecycle.
*   **`+k8s:update=NoModify`**: Use this if you specifically want to enforce that the value cannot change during updates.
*   **`+k8s:update=NoSet`**: Use this if a field cannot be set (transition from nil to non-nil) during an update if it was previously unset.
*   **`+k8s:update=NoUnset`**: Use this if a field cannot be unset (transition from non-nil to nil) during an update if it was previously set.

For the purpose of this "Good First Migration" issue, most fields listed are strictly immutable, so `+k8s:immutable` is the preferred choice unless the existing validation logic explicitly allows transitions (e.g., allow setting once but not modifying afterwards).

### Task List

The following fields have been identified as good candidates for the initial migration.

#### Apps (`apps`)

*   [ ] **ControllerRevision.Data**
    *   **Field:** `Data`
    *   **Location:**
        *   `staging/src/k8s.io/api/apps/v1/types.go`
        *   `staging/src/k8s.io/api/apps/v1beta1/types.go`
        *   `staging/src/k8s.io/api/apps/v1beta2/types.go`
*   [ ] **Deployment.Spec.Selector**
    *   **Field:** `Spec.Selector`
    *   **Location:**
        *   `staging/src/k8s.io/api/apps/v1/types.go`
        *   `staging/src/k8s.io/api/apps/v1beta1/types.go`
        *   `staging/src/k8s.io/api/apps/v1beta2/types.go`
*   [ ] **ReplicaSet.Spec.Selector**
    *   **Field:** `Spec.Selector`
    *   **Location:**
        *   `staging/src/k8s.io/api/apps/v1/types.go`
        *   `staging/src/k8s.io/api/apps/v1beta2/types.go`
*   [x] **StatefulSet.Spec.Selector**
    *   **Field:** `Spec.Selector`
    *   **Location:**
        *   `staging/src/k8s.io/api/apps/v1/types.go`
        *   `staging/src/k8s.io/api/apps/v1beta1/types.go`
        *   `staging/src/k8s.io/api/apps/v1beta2/types.go`

#### Batch (`batch`)

*   [ ] **Job.Spec.Selector**
    *   **Field:** `Spec.Selector`
    *   **Location:**
        *   `staging/src/k8s.io/api/batch/v1/types.go`
        *   `staging/src/k8s.io/api/batch/v1beta1/types.go`

### How to Migrate a Field

1.  **Locate the Versioned Type:** Find the `types.go` file for the versioned API.
2.  **Add the Tag:** Add `// +k8s:immutable` (or `// +k8s:update=NoModify`) above the field definition.
3.  **Generate:** Run `hack/update-codegen.sh validation`.
4.  **Update Strategy:** In the resource's `strategy.go` (usually in `pkg/registry/<group>/<resource>/`), update the `ValidateUpdate` function to use `rest.ValidateUpdateDeclarativelyWithMigrationChecks` (if available/applicable for update validation).
5.  **Verify:**
    *   Ensure unit tests pass.
    *   Run `declarative_validation_test.go` (add one if missing) to prove equivalence.
6.  **Mark Covered:** In the original `validation.go`, find the manual check (typically `apivalidation.ValidateImmutableField`) and append `.MarkCoveredByDeclarative()`.

Example of marking hand-written validation code:
```go
allErrs = append(allErrs, apivalidation.ValidateImmutableField(newObj.Spec.Selector, oldObj.Spec.Selector, fldPath.Child("spec", "selector")).MarkCoveredByDeclarative()...)
```

### Why is this needed?

This helps onboard the community to DV, improves the APIs touched, and helps in the process of getting Declarative Validation to its stated goal of migrating ~50% of existing hand-written code to DV over 5 releases -> improved API readability and more declarative APIs.

title: kubelet memory regression in 1.37: cadvisor housekeeping cannot back off when MemoryQoS sets memory.high
body:
### What happened?

  We observed a 20-30% increase in kubelet RSS memory usage (rate) in OpenShift 5.1 (Kubernetes 1.37) compared to OpenShift 4.23 (Kubernetes 1.36). The root cause is an interaction between the MemoryQoS feature and cadvisor's housekeeping backoff logic.

  MemoryQoS was promoted from alpha (default off) to beta (default on) in Kubernetes 1.37 (pkg/features/kube_features.go:1758 (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/features/kube_features.go#L1758-L1761)), so this regression affects all 1.37 clusters without any explicit opt-in.

  When MemoryQoS is enabled, the kubelet sets memory.high on every non-Guaranteed container's cgroup. This causes the kernel to actively reclaim memory, which continuously increments monotonic counters in memory.stat (pgscan, pgsteal, workingset_refault_file, workingset_refault_anon) and memory.events (high).

  @sohankunkerkar, correctly points out that we see this with MemoryQoS enabling more since cadvisor bumped from v0.56.2 → lib v0.60.5 when Pgscan/Pgsteal/WorkingsetRefault*/Events were added.

cadvisor uses StatsEq() (lib/model/container.go) to decide whether to back off housekeeping frequency. This function calls reflect.DeepEqual(a.Memory, b.Memory) on the full MemoryStats struct, which includes those monotonic counters.
  Since the counters change every tick, StatsEq always returns false, preventing cadvisor from backing off beyond the baseline housekeeping interval.

  The kubelet overrides cadvisor's default housekeeping_interval from 1s to 10s (pkg/kubelet/cadvisor/cadvisor_linux.go:67-74 (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/cadvisor/cadvisor_linux.go#L67-L74)), with a maxHousekeepingInterval of 15s. The backoff progression is 10s → 15s. When StatsEq returns false, the interval resets to the 10s baseline instead of reaching 15s. This means every container is polled every 10s instead of 15s — 50% more cgroup I/O per container than expected at steady state.

  The result is increased housekeeping overhead per container, causing:
  - +40% allocation churn (measured: 11.3 MB/s vs 8.1 MB/s baseline)
  - More bufio.Scanner allocations reading cgroup files (+49%)
  - More gRPC CRI calls for container status (+46%)
  - Cascading volume manager reconciliation (+66%)
## Fix

Replace reflect.DeepEqual(a.Memory, b.Memory) in StatsEq() with a field-by-field comparison that only checks usage-level fields (Usage, RSS, Cache, WorkingSet, Swap, etc.) and excludes monotonic counters (Pgscan, Pgsteal, WorkingsetRefault*, Failcnt, Events, PSI).

cadvisor PR: https://github.com/google/cadvisor/pull/3944

### What did you expect to happen?

Near even allocation changes within the Kubelet.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

* [Unit test](https://github.com/google/cadvisor/pull/3944/changes#diff-62aa1d0042e7a1578633595116318fe3f68a90c5124f5f582e00f83e90643dd9) in cadvisor
* [OpenShift cadvisor PR under test](https://github.com/openshift/kubernetes/pull/2814)
* [OpenShift CI successful run](https://pr-payload-tests.ci.openshift.org/runs/ci/9bfe71a0-c35b-11f1-8386-124a4ecb37fb-0)
* [OpenShift Jira Issue](https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPBUGS-129642)
* [Test Memory QOS](https://gist.github.com/rphillips/e538ef42db8b66b53f00cd2fab12697d) This gist can be run with the cadvisor patch, and enabling/disabling MemoryQoS to try the different variations. I ran it locally a number of times to gather data.

title: node_e2e: Cleanup configuration and rename jenkins/ directory
body:
/kind cleanup
/sig node
/area test
/priority important-longterm
/assign

Currently, node_e2e configuration exists in the `jenkins/` directory underneath node_e2e. This directory is a hangover from the time before Kubernetes migrated to Prow. This directory is regularly a point of contention when adding new features to tests, and causes confusion to people trying to make changes to them.

We should remove the unused portions of this directory and rename it to something more useful (`e2e_node/configuration`?) to simplify future changes while maintaining the current developer workflow.

This is going to involve coordinating a couple of things between k/k and k/test-infra to ensure that we do not cause a break in tests during the migration process and to not break running tests against older release branches.

My naive suggestion for handling this would be:

- [ ] Remove unused code from jenkins/
- [ ] Create a copy of the jenkins/ directory with the new name
- [ ] Update test-infra to reference the new paths, duplicating configurations where necessary to preserve jobs for older branches
- [ ] Remove the jenkins/ directory

(@spiffxp / @dims might have better suggestions for how to handle this?)

title: WorkloadWithJob: Jobs with names of 58+ characters never start because the PodGroupTemplate name exceeds 63 bytes
body:
### What happened?

With `WorkloadWithJob` enabled, a Job whose name is 58+ characters never starts pods. The Job controller names the PodGroupTemplate `<job-name>-pgt-0` ([job_scheduling_manager.go#L518-L521](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0887d3330e9bb0489dac763160f2ca27702e7729/pkg/controller/job/job_scheduling_manager.go#L518-L521)), and `spec.podGroupTemplates[].name` is a DNS label limited to 63 bytes ([types.go#L218](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0887d3330e9bb0489dac763160f2ca27702e7729/staging/src/k8s.io/api/scheduling/v1beta1/types.go#L218)). Workload creation is rejected and the Job requeues forever:

```
Workload.scheduling.k8s.io "<job>-65657c449d" is invalid: spec.podGroupTemplates[0].name: Invalid value: "<job>-pgt-0": must be no more than 63 bytes
```

The Workload/PodGroup object names are already truncated and hashed ([names.go#L34-L50](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0887d3330e9bb0489dac763160f2ca27702e7729/staging/src/k8s.io/component-helpers/scheduling/schedulingv1/workloadbuilder/names.go#L34-L50)), but the template name is not.

### What did you expect to happen?

Any valid Job name (up to 63 characters) gets a valid Workload and PodGroup, and the Job runs.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Enable `GenericWorkload` and `WorkloadWithJob`, enable `scheduling.k8s.io/v1beta1`, then:

```sh
kubectl create job $(printf 'a%.0s' {1..58}) --image=busybox -- true
kubectl get events --field-selector reason=FailedWorkloadCreate
```

A 57-character name works; 58 and 63 fail.

### Anything else we need to know?

The template name is local to the Workload, so it doesn't need to embed the Job name at all. A fixed or bounded name (e.g. `pgt-0`, or a truncated prefix plus a hash) would avoid the limit. Existing Workloads reference the current name, so a change has to keep finding templates that already exist.

title: Swap e2e "Basic functionality" LimitedSwap tests can't fail
body:
### What happened?

While looking into #138226 I noticed the LimitedSwap QoS tests in `test/e2e_node/swap_test.go` don't actually test anything. There are two bugs:

1. `getSwapTestPod` builds `resources` for the requested QoS class but never puts them on the pod. It's just returned `getSleepingPod(...)` since 2230ed7dc6a, so every entry runs a BestEffort pod. You can see it in both swap CI jobs, where Burstable and Guaranteed log:
   `Calculating swap for burstable pods: ... containerMemoryRequest: 0, swapAllocation: 0`
   (e.g. [ubuntu run](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-node-swap-conformance-ubuntu-serial/2108165536956289024) and [crio run](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-node-crio-swap-serial/2108202027736633344))

2. `expectLimitedSwap` checks the limit with `gomega.Or(>= expected-4Ki, <= expected+4Ki)`, which matches any number. I checked it with expected = 128Mi and it accepts 0 and 1TiB.

### What did you expect to happen?

Each entry should run a pod of the QoS class it names, and the swap limit check should use `And`.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Grep any swap serial job's build log for "Calculating swap for burstable pods": the request is always 0. For the matcher:
```go
m := gomega.Or(gomega.BeNumerically(">=", 128<<20-4096), gomega.BeNumerically("<=", 128<<20+4096))
ok, _ := m.Match(0) // true
```

### Anything else we need to know?

Fixing both will make the Guaranteed and "request equals limit" entries fail as written. `calcSwapForBurstablePod` expects a non-zero limit for them, but the kubelet correctly gives them no swap, so the expected value has to be 0 unless the pod is Burstable with a memory request that differs from its limit. The NodeConformance entries use `getSwapTestPod` too.

### Which jobs are flaking?

pull-kubernetes-unit-windows-master


### Which tests are flaking?

TestCIDRAllocateNextConcurrentWithRelease
package: k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/registry/core/service/ipallocator
file: pkg/registry/core/service/ipallocator/cidrallocator_test.go


### Since when has it been flaking?

Since d8d5b004c2bd9cecaa82c7077c87f60691157675 (PR #142758, merged 2026-10-06)
"ipallocator: use RWMutex for ServiceCIDR map and thread-safe rand"


### Testgrid link

https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/pr-logs/pull/140855/pull-kubernetes-unit-windows-master/2108320062355017728

### Reason for failure (if possible)

The test panics with "channel full" raised from `RaceFreeFakeWatcher.Add` (staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/watch/watch.go:253).

The fake clientset's `ObjectTracker` hands out watchers backed by a fixed 100-event channel (`watch.DefaultChanSize`) and delivers events with a non-blocking send that panics when the channel is full.

`TestCIDRAllocateNextConcurrentWithRelease` runs 50 goroutines x 10 rounds of allocate+release, producing ~1000 watch events. On a busy/slow CI machine (Windows presubmits are especially prone) the informer reflector does not consume events fast enough, the 100-event channel overflows, and the whole
test binary panics.

This is a test-infrastructure flake, not a production bug: the production `MetaAllocator` code is fine; the fake watch plumbing in the test harness cannot absorb the event volume the test generates under CPU contention. Reproduced locally with `GOMAXPROCS=2` (and even `GOMAXPROCS=1`).

### Anything else we need to know?

`TestCIDRAllocateNextConcurrent` (same file, same harness) is exposed to the same failure mode.

title: kube-scheduler waits indefinitely when GenericWorkload is enabled but its API is disabled
body:
## What happened?

Enabling `GenericWorkload=true` on the control-plane components without enabling `scheduling.k8s.io/v1beta1` on kube-apiserver leaves kube-scheduler running but unready. Scheduling is blocked for ordinary Pods, even when no Workloads or PodGroups have been created.

The API server starts successfully and passes `/readyz`. Scheduling API discovery only advertises `scheduling.k8s.io/v1`, and `/apis/scheduling.k8s.io/v1beta1/podgroups` returns 404.

The scheduler repeatedly logs:

```text
"Failed to watch" err="failed to list *v1beta1.PodGroup: the server could not find the requested resource"
```

Its `/readyz?verbose` endpoint returns HTTP 500:

```text
[+]leaderElection ok
[+]shutdown ok
[-]sched-handler-sync failed: reason withheld
readyz check failed
```

In an isolated single-node kind cluster, kube-apiserver and kube-controller-manager were `1/1 Running`, but kube-scheduler was `0/1 Running`. CoreDNS, kindnet, kube-proxy, and local-path-provisioner remained Pending with no assigned node. kind timed out waiting for the node to become Ready.

Kube-controller-manager also repeatedly logged the missing-PodGroup API error, although the manager process itself passed readiness.

## What did you expect to happen?

Most rebases we never have to coordinate the merge of changes for kubeapiserver with the feature gate.
This seems to be a potential issue for upgrades.

## Discussion Questions

Should we handle the API not being enabled gracefully and fall back even if feature gate is enabled?

## How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Use a Kubernetes build whose GenericWorkload scheduler consumes PodGroups through `scheduling.k8s.io/v1beta1`.

Create `generic-workload.yaml`:

```yaml
kind: Cluster
apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4
featureGates:
  GenericWorkload: true
nodes:
- role: control-plane
```

Build a kind node image from the Kubernetes source revision to test, then create an isolated cluster:

```sh
kind build node-image --type source --image kindest/node:generic-workload-test .
kind create cluster \
  --name generic-workload-repro \
  --image kindest/node:generic-workload-test \
  --config generic-workload.yaml \
  --kubeconfig ./generic-workload.kubeconfig \
  --retain --wait 60s
export KUBECONFIG="$PWD/generic-workload.kubeconfig"
```

## Anything else we need to know?

### Control cases and workaround

| GenericWorkload | Scheduling v1beta1 API served | Scheduler result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Enabled | No | HTTP 500 readiness; ordinary Pods remain unscheduled |
| Enabled | Yes | HTTP 200 readiness; waiting Pods are scheduled |
| Disabled | No | HTTP 200 readiness |

All three combinations were checked in the isolated cluster. Adding only this kube-apiserver flag allowed the existing scheduler to finish startup and acquire its leader lease without restarting the scheduler:

```text
--runtime-config=scheduling.k8s.io/v1beta1=true
```

For a new kind cluster, add this top-level setting alongside `featureGates`:

```yaml
runtimeConfig:
  scheduling.k8s.io/v1beta1: "true"
```

### Source analysis

- `pkg/controlplane/instance.go` disables `scheduling.k8s.io/v1beta1` by default.
- `pkg/registry/scheduling/rest/storage_scheduling.go` requires both API-resource enablement and the feature gate before installing PodGroup storage.
- `pkg/scheduler/eventhandlers.go` registers the v1beta1 PodGroup informer whenever `GenericWorkload` is enabled, without checking API availability.
- `cmd/kube-scheduler/app/server.go` waits for informer cache synchronization before completing startup and entering scheduling. Repeated 404s prevent the PodGroup informer from synchronizing; there is no configuration-specific timeout or diagnostic.
- The PodGroup protection controller and resource claim controller also wait for PodGroup cache synchronization when this feature is enabled.

## AI assistance disclosure

AI assistance was used to reproduce the behavior in an isolated cluster, analyze the relevant Kubernetes source paths, and draft this issue.

title: Make `conversion-gen` automatically pick up autogenerated conversion functions of types across packages
body:
### What happened?

Right now, if you have a cross-package type reference, e.g. the `authorization.k8s.io` type `AuthorizationConditionsRequest` refers to `AdmissionRequest` in `admission.k8s.io`, `conversion-gen` fails with

```go
	if in.AdmissionRequest != nil {
		in, out := &in.AdmissionRequest, &out.AdmissionRequest
		*out = new(admission.AdmissionRequest)
		// FIXME: Provide conversion function to convert admissionv1.AdmissionRequest to admission.AdmissionRequest
		compileErrorOnMissingConversion()
	} else {
		out.AdmissionRequest = nil
	}
```

in the generated code on the `authorization.k8s.io` side. This is because `conversion-gen` doesn't "see" any ready-made conversion for `AdmissionRequest` between its internal and external versions. However, `conversion-gen` is in fact responsible for generating that conversion too, hence it doesn't exist up front.

This can be worked around by adding the following to `pkg/apis/admission/v1/conversion.go`:

```go
// Convert_v1_AdmissionRequest_To_admission_AdmissionRequest just calls the covering autogenerated function, but is defined and thus
// "exported" in conversion.go, such that it is usable by other API groups that embed AdmissionRequest.
func Convert_v1_AdmissionRequest_To_admission_AdmissionRequest(in *admissionv1.AdmissionRequest, out *admission.AdmissionRequest, s conversion.Scope) error {
	return autoConvert_v1_AdmissionRequest_To_admission_AdmissionRequest(in, out, s)
}

// Convert_admission_AdmissionRequest_To_v1_AdmissionRequest just calls the covering autogenerated function, but is defined and thus
// "exported" in conversion.go, such that it is usable by other API groups that embed AdmissionRequest.
func Convert_admission_AdmissionRequest_To_v1_AdmissionRequest(in *admission.AdmissionRequest, out *admissionv1.AdmissionRequest, s conversion.Scope) error {
	return autoConvert_admission_AdmissionRequest_To_v1_AdmissionRequest(in, out, s)
}
```

### What did you expect to happen?

I want `conversion-gen` to understand what `Convert_X_Z_To_Y_Z` functions it will generate, and call those automatically when creating the conversions.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Consider the type structure e.g. in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/137633
Make a cross-API-package type reference in core Kubernetes, and try to generate a conversion.

title: Expose per-resource storage write revision metric for watch cache and informer lag
body:
[WatchCacheLag](https://perf-dash.k8s.io/#/?jobname=gce-5000Nodes&metriccategoryname=GenericMeasurements&metricname=WatchCacheLag) and InformerCacheLag compare `apiserver_watch_cache_resource_version` against the global `etcd_debugging_mvcc_current_revision`.

When a resource has no writes while other resources mutate, its watch cache RV stays at the last write until an etcd bookmark arrives. Because etcd bookmarks are infrequent, P99 lag is inflated idle phases (see graph below for services. The flat 0s at beginning and end are the only time services are changed, and sawtooth happens during times without writes.)

![Watch cache delay sawtooth during idle resource phases](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Jefftree/kubernetes/issue-assets/watch_cache_lag_services.png)

We should record the last written storage revision per resource (e.g. `apiserver_storage_resource_version{group, resource}`) on successful writes in [etcd3/store.go](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/store.go) and compare `apiserver_watch_cache_resource_version` against that metric instead of the global etcd revision.

title: kube-scheduler: a hung HTTP extender limits scheduling to one pod per httpTimeout, even with ignorable: true
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Stop calling an HTTP extender for a while after its calls keep failing, so that a hung extender does not cost every pod a full `httpTimeout`.

Today every scheduling cycle calls every interested extender synchronously and waits until the call returns or times out (`http.Client.Timeout = httpTimeout`, `pkg/scheduler/extender.go`):

- Filter: `findNodesThatPassExtenders` calls `Filter`; with `ignorable: true` an error is logged and the extender is skipped for this pod only (`pkg/scheduler/schedule_one.go`).
- Prioritize: `prioritizeNodes` waits for all extender goroutines; an error is logged at V(5) and the extender's scores are dropped for this pod only.

The next pod calls the same extender again and waits again. Nothing remembers that the previous call timed out a moment ago.

A possible shape (open to other designs):

1. Per extender, count consecutive failed calls (transport errors and timeouts). After N consecutive failures (for example 3), skip the extender for a backoff period that grows from 1s up to 30-60s. While skipped, behave exactly as on an error today: an ignorable filter is skipped, a prioritizer gives no scores. When the backoff ends, the next pod probes the extender; a successful call resets the counter.
2. Apply it only where an error is already tolerated: ignorable extenders and the prioritize verb, whose errors are always tolerated. Non-ignorable filter and bind keep failing loudly, as intended in #60616.
3. Make it visible: a metric with extender call duration and result per extender and verb, and a log line (or metric) when an extender enters and leaves backoff. Today a failing prioritizer is visible only at `-v=5`.

While the extender is down the scheduling result is the same as today; only the time spent waiting changes. The difference is during recovery: an extender that comes back is used again after at most one backoff period. If that needs to be configurable, it could be an optional field on `Extender` (for example `failureBackoff`).

### Why is this needed?

A hung extender, one that accepts the connection and never answers (GC pause, deadlock, CPU starvation, a network path dropping packets), is a realistic failure. While it lasts, scheduler throughput for the whole cluster drops to about one pod per `httpTimeout`. `ignorable: true` does not help here: it only decides what happens after the timeout.

Measured on kube-scheduler v1.35.9 (1 control-plane node with 4 vCPU, 3 worker nodes), one prioritize-only HTTPS extender (`nodeCacheCapable: true`, `ignorable: true`, `httpTimeout: 2s`, `weight: 2`), bursts of 100 pause pods (1m CPU / 4Mi), median of 3 runs:

| Extender state | Pods bound per second |
| --- | --- |
| No extender configured | about 20 (1) |
| Healthy | 12.0 (11.4..13.9) |
| Service without endpoints (connection refused) | 11.2 (10.7..18.3) |
| Process stopped with SIGSTOP (TCP accepted, no response) | 0.5: 100 pods in 201.7 s, median interval between bindings 2.01 s, p50 create-to-bound 99.6 s |

(1) Bursts of 100 pods without an extender were bimodal on this control-plane node (16-18 or 32-36 pods/s, depending on its load). The medians of 250-pod bursts without an extender stayed within 20.4-21.6 pods/s over four days, so about 20 is the steady figure. The hung-extender row does not depend on it: it is bounded by `httpTimeout`, 1 pod per 2 s.

A refused connection fails fast and costs little. A hung extender costs the full timeout on every pod. Lowering `httpTimeout` reduces the damage, but it trades against the extender's legitimate tail latency, and the damage still grows with the number of pods to schedule.

Steps to reproduce:

1. Configure a prioritize-only extender with `ignorable: true` and `httpTimeout: 2s`.
2. Send `SIGSTOP` to the extender process.
3. Create 100 pods and measure the time until they are bound.

We are happy to send a PR once the shape is agreed.

/sig scheduling
/kind feature

title: Watch cache shrinks before burst scale-up
body:
### What happened? /sig api-machinery /assign We are load-testing and tuning the performance of our clusters, and we have observed an unusual behavior. Under sustained bursty traffic, contrary to what we would normally expect, the watch cache size is repeatedly and rapidly halved, and then quickly scaled back up. See figure below. This may cause several problems: 1. The watch cache size is directly related to the watcher channel size. When a burst arrives, some clients may request with a small watcher channel size. Once the channel buffer becomes full and blocks over 50ms, the API server terminates those watch connections. This has in fact occurred in our environment: our monitoring shows increases in both terminated watchers and initial events. 2. Every cache resize requires acquiring a lock and copying memory. This operation is relatively expensive, so repeated scale-down and scale-up cycles should ideally be avoided. This traffic pattern is realistic in our environment because we operate clusters for long-running AI workloads, where Pods may be created or updated in bursts. Would it make sense to introduce a hysteresis mechanism? For example, if the interval between the two most recent events is significantly shorter than the historical average inter-event interval, the buffer could temporarily avoid scaling down. Below, I used AI to help me to generate some sample data and charts to illustrate how the cache size changes under different traffic patterns, both with and without this mechanism. These results may help evaluate whether such a change would improve the resizing behavior. see figure below: It is also worth noting that, although this algorithm does not directly fix the issue described in [[#139250](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/139250)](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/139250), it may still provide benefits for certain traffic patterns. see figure above`3a`. In particular, it can prevent a burst from causing rapid cache expansion followed by a state where the buffer no longer satisfies the `full` condition, leaving the cache unable to scale down even when additional events arrive. ### What did you expect to happen? when burst requests arrive, do not half the cache size and scale it back. ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? 1. Continuously create or update Pods at a high rate until the monitored watch cache size reaches its maximum. 2. Leave the cluster idle for a period of time. The required duration depends on the timeout configured for the API server. 3. Rapidly create or update Pods again, and observe that the monitored watch cache size is quickly halved before growing back to its maximum. ### Anything else we need to know? _No response_ ### Kubernetes version

title: kubectl config set/unset panics with "reflect: Elem of invalid type runtime.Object" on extensions paths
body:
### What happened?

`kubectl config set` and `kubectl config unset` panic when the property path goes into an `extensions` map:

```
$ kubectl config set clusters.foo.extensions.bar x --kubeconfig /tmp/kc
panic: reflect: Elem of invalid type runtime.Object
```

Exit code 2. The same happens for `extensions.foo`, `preferences.extensions.foo`, `users.<name>.extensions.foo` and `contexts.<name>.extensions.foo`, with both `set` and `unset`.

/sig cli
/kind bug


### What did you expect to happen?

An error saying the path can't be set, the way other unsupported paths are handled (for example `users.foo.exec.command` returns `unable to parse one or more field values of ...`).


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

```sh
cat > /tmp/kc <<'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Config
clusters:
- name: foo
  cluster:
    server: https://x
EOF
kubectl config set clusters.foo.extensions.bar x --kubeconfig /tmp/kc
kubectl config unset preferences.extensions.foo --kubeconfig /tmp/kc
```

title: Optimize Topology-Aware Scheduling for CompositePodGroups with identical children
body:
### What would you like to be added?


Topology-Aware Scheduling (TAS) for CompositePodGroups currently schedules child workloads sequentially in `compositePodGroupSchedulingDefaultAlgorithm`:
- **Enumerate candidate placements**: For each child PodGroup (or nested CompositePodGroup), enumerate all candidate topology domains (e.g., zones, racks, or nodes) matching the group's topology constraints.
- **Evaluate candidate placements from scratch**: Iterate through every candidate placement, running simulated pod scheduling (`SignPod`, `PreFilter`, `Filter`, `Score`, and tentative `Reserve`) across candidate nodes, and computing placement scores via `PlacementScore` plugins.
- **Select best placement and commit**: Normalize placement scores, select the highest-scoring candidate (breaking ties randomly), tentatively commit the child's placement to the snapshot, and advance to the next child.

When scheduling CompositePodGroups representing distributed workloads (e.g., distributed AI/ML training or HPC jobs), the hierarchy frequently consists of multiple identical child PodGroups (e.g., homogeneous worker groups with identical pod templates, resource requests, and topology constraints).
While kube-scheduler already employs opportunistic batching at the **pod/node level** (KEP-5598: reusing node evaluation outcomes across consecutive identical pods and invalidating only the chosen node), no equivalent mechanism exists at the **PodGroup/placement level**.

Because candidate placements are evaluated independently from scratch for every child in the hierarchy:
- The scheduler re-evaluates feasibility and re-runs placement scoring plugins across all candidate placements for each child, even though cluster state and capacity outside the previously selected placement remain unchanged.
- For a CompositePodGroup with $M$ child groups and $P$ candidate placements, this results in $O(M \times P)$ simulated placement evaluations. On large clusters (e.g., thousands of nodes across tens of racks or zones), this produces thousands of redundant placement evaluations.
- Non-overlapping candidate placements (placements that share no nodes with the placement selected by the previous child) retain identical feasibility and raw placement scores, but are discarded and re-evaluated from scratch in each child iteration.

As a result, the scheduler spends significant time in redundant placement simulation, leading to:
- High scheduling latency for CompositePodGroup workloads (e.g., spending dozens to hundreds of seconds in `scheduler_podgroup_scheduling_algorithm_duration_seconds`).
- Excessive CPU and memory consumption in the scheduler from repeated pod filtering and scoring across unaffected nodes.
- Head-of-line blocking in the scheduler queue for subsequent workloads waiting for scheduling cycles.

### Proposed solution

Conceptually, the proposed solution **lifts opportunistic batching (KEP-5598) from the pod/node level to the PodGroup/placement level**: instead of evaluating individual nodes for consecutive identical pods, it caches candidate topology placements across consecutive identical child PodGroups (or nested CompositePodGroups).

We propose introducing placement result and score caching in `scheduleOnePodGroup` for CompositePodGroups (guarded by an alpha feature gate `TopologyAwareCompositePodGroupOptimization`) that:
1. **Detect identical consecutive child groups**: Check equivalence between consecutive children (`arePodGroupsIdenticalWithRoot` / cached `QueuedPodInfo.PodSignature`) to determine if candidate placement evaluations can be reused across child iterations.
2. **Cache placement feasibility and unweighted raw scores**: Split placement scoring in the framework into raw plugin scoring (`RunRawPlacementScorePlugins`, computing raw scores in $[0, \text{MaxPlacementScore}]$) and normalization (`NormalizePlacementScores`). Cache feasibility outcomes and raw scores across candidate placements for identical child groups.
3. **Invalidate only overlapping candidate placements**: When child $i$ selects placement $p_{\text{last}}$, identify and invalidate only candidate placements that overlap (share nodes) with $p_{\text{last}}$ (analogous to invalidating the selected node in pod-level opportunistic batching). All non-overlapping candidate placements reuse their cached feasibility and raw plugin scores.
4. **Recalculate affected placements and re-normalize scores**: Re-evaluate feasibility and raw scores only for invalidated overlapping placements, update the cache, re-normalize scores across all surviving feasible placements, and break ties randomly to preserve identical placement distribution and quality.
5. **Support multi-level hierarchies**: Recursively propagate placement caching across both leaf `PodGroup`s and nested child `CompositePodGroup`s.

The AI based POC implementing this approach is available on [44past4/kubernetes:cpg-tas-optimization](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/compare/master...44past4:kubernetes:cpg-tas-optimization?diff=unified&w) branch (with benchmarks added to `test/integration/scheduler_perf/cpg/cpg_test.go`).

### Why is this needed?

Minimizing scheduling algorithm latency for large multi-gang workloads is essential for cluster throughput and resource utilization. The current algorithm results in:
- High algorithmic latency scaling quadratically with the number of identical child groups and candidate topology domains.
- Thousands of redundant simulated placement evaluations on nodes whose capacity and state are unchanged.
- Head-of-line queue delay for subsequent workloads in multi-tenant environments.

Extending the opportunistic batching principles of KEP-5598 from the pod/node level to the PodGroup/placement level eliminates these redundant evaluations while preserving identical placement quality and scoring semantics.

In [scheduler performance benchmarks](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1USEVtKRIKcOBdsa26qfaSGFMif4HlFVqcvtijAGx4hA/edit?usp=sharing) on a 5,000-node cluster (5 zones, 50 racks) with CompositePodGroups of 4 to 128 child groups:
- Placement feasibility evaluations were reduced by **`3.05x` to `35.56x`** (e.g., `12,800 → 360` evaluations for 256 PodGroups across 50 racks).
- Pure TAS algorithm execution time (`scheduler_podgroup_scheduling_algorithm_duration_seconds`) was reduced by **`64.1%` to `95.4%`** (**`2.79x` to `21.71x` speedup**).
- End-to-end workload scheduling duration improved by **`2.45x` to `3.90x`** with identical placement distribution.

title: resourceclaim controller: deleted claims stay visible in the MutationCache for up to 1h
body:
The controller's claim MutationCache (`pkg/controller/resourceclaim/controller.go:356`) uses `IncludeAdds: true` with a 1h TTL, but the claim informer handlers never call `OnAddOrUpdate`/`OnDelete`. After a generated claim is deleted and the informer observes it, `claimExists` and `findPodResourceClaim` still return it from the mutation cache, so the controller does not recreate it until the entry expires.

Reproduced at 4dfdf5067a2 with a unit test (mutation, API delete, wait for informer, `claimExists` returns true); wiring the informer events the way #140063 did for the ResourceSlice controller fixes it. `claimExists` came with #140227 and is in v1.37.

/wg device-management
/kind bug

title: Workload-Aware Preemption may result in unnecessary or cascading preemptions
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Workload-aware (PodGroup) preemption currently operates in three steps during PodGroupPostFilter:
- **Remove all potential victims**: Identify all lower-priority workloads/pods in the cluster that the preempting PodGroup is eligible to preempt and remove them from the scheduling snapshot upfront.
- **Speculatively schedule the preemptor**: Run the standard PodGroup scheduling algorithm on this stripped snapshot to find a feasible node assignment for all pods in the preempting PodGroup.
- **Reprieve unnecessary victims**: Iterate through the removed victims (ordered from most important to least important via MoreImportantVictim) and restore any victim that can still coexist with the chosen PodGroup placement; evict the remaining victims.

During step 2, because all potential victims have already been removed from the snapshot, standard Score plugins cannot distinguish between:
- Nodes that already have sufficient free capacity (requiring no preemption).
- Nodes where capacity was only freed by removing high-priority or large PodGroup victims versus low-priority or small victims.
- Nodes whose victims have already been condemned by an earlier pod in the same preempting PodGroup (especially when preempting a victim PodGroup with DisruptionMode: PodGroup frees spots across multiple nodes).

As a result, the scheduler treats all freed nodes equally and scatters the preempting PodGroup across occupied and empty nodes alike. Step 3 (reprieveVictim) can only save victims on nodes that were not selected in Step 2, leading to:
- Unnecessary preemption of victims even when free nodes exist in the cluster.
- Preemption of higher-priority or larger workloads when lower-priority victims could have been chosen instead.
- Cascading disruption of multiple victim PodGroups instead of reusing spots freed by already-condemned victim PodGroups.


### Proposed solution
Introduce victim-aware node scoring in DefaultPreemption active only during PodGroup preemption evaluation that:
1. Track surviving vs. condemned victims across the PodGroup scheduling pass
2. Compute per-node incremental ("delta") victims in PreScore
3. Prioritize nodes by preemption cost in Score, assigning the maximum score (100) to nodes that require no new victims (either genuinely free nodes or nodes whose victims were already condemned by an earlier pod in the PodGroup), deferring tie-breaking among zero-cost nodes to standard Score plugins.
For nodes where preemption is required, we score them accordingly to the "importance" of the victims  - the more important victims needs to be preempted (priority, size, etc.), the lower the score of that node is.

The POC implementing this approach is in: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142325 (together with the results from the benchmarks being introduced in: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142679 ).

### Why is this needed?

Minimizing the "cost" of preemptions is the goal for all users and current algorithm may result in:
- Unnecessary preemption of victims even when free nodes exist in the cluster.
- Preemption of higher-priority or larger workloads when lower-priority victims could have been chosen instead.
- Cascading disruption of multiple victim PodGroups instead of reusing spots freed by already-condemned victim PodGroups.

which isn't acceptable for many users.

title: WAS: Gang-schedule Pods that are created in order, like in MPI bootstrap
body:
### What would you like to be added?

 A way for a gang PodGroup or CompositePodGroup to account for Pods that its owning controller intentionally creates later, after other Pods in the group are already running/complete.

Today the scheduler holds a gang's Pods until minCount of them exist on the control plane. That doesn't work for workloads with ordering dependencies inside one gang. The main example is MPI training through Kubeflow Trainer and JobSet: https://github.com/kubeflow/trainer/pull/3219#discussion_r4171153558

- The TrainJob runtime has two ReplicatedJobs: launcher and node
- With `runLauncherAsNode: true`, the launcher is rank 0. The node ReplicatedJob runs numNodes - 1 workers
- `mpirun` needs every worker's SSH server up before it starts, so JobSet only creates the launcher Pod once all workers are Ready (we [use dependsOn API for that](https://github.com/kubeflow/trainer/blob/master/manifests/base/runtimes/deepspeed_distributed.yaml#L61))
 - For one gang across launcher and workers (same topology domain, all-or-nothing), the natural setting is minCount = numNodes
 
That deadlocks. The workers wait for minCount Pods to exist before they're scheduled. The launcher Pod isn't created until the workers are Ready.

Some possible directions (open to SIG Scheduling's input):

1. Declared-but-deferred members: let a PodGroupTemplate/PodGroup declare how many extra Pods it expects later and what resources they need (for example, a reference to a Pod template or a resource shape). The scheduler would then reserve capacity for them in the chosen placement/topology domain once minCount existing Pods are schedulable.
2. Separate "gang admission count" from "reservation count": for example, keep minCount as the threshold for releasing Pods, and add a separate field for the total number of Pods (or resources) to reserve.
3. Ordered sub-groups within one Workload: let a later sub-group (the launcher) join an earlier sub-group's placement once the earlier one has been scheduled, with its capacity held in the meantime. This could build on CompositePodGroup.

I would expect we will see similar problems with [initializers or data cache](https://trainer.kubeflow.org/en/latest/user-guides/data-cache.html#architecture), when training job waits until initializer Job is complete (cc @akshaychitneni).


### Why is this needed?

  - WAS doesn't support ordered bootstrap. MPI (launcher/worker) can't be gang-scheduled with a minCount that covers the whole job. The scheduler waits for minCount Pods to exist, but the driver Pod is only created after the workers are Ready, so the job deadlocks.
- The current workaround is lossy. In https://github.com/kubeflow/trainer/pull/3219, Kubeflow Trainer plans to leave dependent ReplicatedJobs out of minCount. The launcher still joins the same PodGroup and can land in the same topology domain, but its capacity isn't reserved. On a busy cluster, the workers can be gang-scheduled and hold GPUs while the launcher stays Pending.


cc @kannon92 @tenzen-y @mm4tt @robert-bell

title: APF Request Cost Model: Tune Seat Estimation to Allocations
body:
### What would you like to be added?

As a follow-up and complement to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/142223
 and https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/132233, we propose updating APF work estimation to reflect object estimations with a semi automated process of updating the estimates when needed.

Instead of a bespoke and manual process of adjusting request costs like we did just for large LISTs, we should standardize the process of estimating request cost that can be easier to automate and cover other methods.

Using standardized exemplar object shapes like https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/138415 and measuring allocations allows us to create a deterministic process of comparing request costs across different methods and serialization formats. We see allocations as a natural extension to the current request cost model that accounts not only for maximum live memory, but also for the additional asynchronous GC work (mark-assist and sweep contention) that is not proportional to synchronous CPU duration (seats * time) yet can be deterministically measured.

We imagine a simple benchmark that runs a for loop that executes each type of request one by one and uses metrics to measure allocations on apiserver. 

The seat assignment will now be a combination of maximum live memory, number of allocations (mallocs), and allocated bytes (allocMB) while handling a request (mapped to the signals available at admission time: input/average object size, estimated object count, and watcher count). Like before, we will separate two types of requests—streamed (WatchList and LIST with streaming responses) and non-streamed—and use different seat calculations for them based on the worst case. The seat cost will be renormalized to allow the same baseline number of requests as before.

Based on our experiments, using this method better represents the real request cost (reducing the worst-case LIST cost-per-seat discrepancy from 222x down to 3.3x) and allows up to 3x more cheap requests, while detecting and punishing unexpected heavyweights (5x–50x).

### Why is this needed?

Ensure we can systematically detect and price unexpected, allocation-heavy requests ("allocation mines") such as:

* PATCH vs. PUT: Both are charged 1 seat, yet PATCH does 2–3x more allocations than PUT on the happy path  and nearly 30x more allocations  during in-place GuaranteedUpdate transaction conflicts.
* WATCH opened on an older RV: Charged 1 seat, yet replaying history from the watch cache ring buffer does not benefit from the cachingObject serialization cache and calls DeepCopyObject() per event—requiring 100–160x more allocations than a live watcher.
* WatchList vs. Streaming LIST: Charged the same 10 seats as LIST based on peak memory, yet WatchList allocates 3–8x more bytes and 2–2.5x more objects due to DeepCopyObject() of initial events—cutting sustained kube-apiserver throughput in half and doubling P99 latency.
* No separation of DELETECOLLECTION with seats defaults to 1 seat despite allocating per object deleted 

The goal is that by systematically detecting high-allocation paths and increasing their seat cost, giving visibility to inefficient paths and motivating their optimization thus prevent hitting the Go runtime allocation ceiling (discussed in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/142223
). While we will optimize those paths over time, APF is the only mechanism that can prevent degradation of kube-apiserver performance in the meantime.

---

### Benchmark Data (For `10KB` Exemplar Pod)

#### 1. Collection & Watch Methods (Allocations per `10KB` Pod Returned)

| Request (`10KB` Exemplar Pod) | Per-Object Seat Calculation in APF? | Alloc Bytes / Pod | Alloc Objects / Pod | Ratio vs. `LIST ?rv=0` (Bytes / Objs) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`LIST ?resourceVersion=0` (Streamed)** | Yes (capped at `1 MB`) | **`2.18 KB / pod`** | **`49 objs / pod`** | **`1.0x / 1.0x` (Baseline)** |
| **`WATCH ?watch=true&resourceVersion=<current_RV>`** | No (live stream) | `0.09 KB / pod` | `0.7 objs / pod` | `0.04x / 0.01x` |

title: Potential goroutine leak in client-go/tools/remotecommand/websocket.go
apimachinery yaml: YAMLOrJSONDecoder drops a trailing document shorter than 4 bytes
body:
### What happened?

`YAMLOrJSONDecoder` fails to decode a document when fewer than 4 bytes remain in the stream. The same document decodes correctly if a single trailing space is added.

```
"{a}"          len=3  ->  error: json: offset 2: invalid character 'a' looking for beginning of object key string
"{a} "         len=4  ->  map[a:<nil>]
"{ab}"         len=4  ->  map[ab:<nil>]

`{"a":1}{b}`   ->  doc 1 decodes, doc 2 fails   (3 bytes remaining)
`{"a":1}{bc}`  ->  doc 1 decodes, doc 2 decodes (4 bytes remaining)
```

The cutoff is exactly 4 bytes, which is the read size in `consumeWhitespace`.

`consumeWhitespace` (`staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/yaml/decoder.go:362`) discards a short read:

```go
buf, err := d.stream.ReadN(4)
if err != nil && err == io.EOF { //nolint:errorlint
	return err
}
```

`ReadN` documents the opposite contract:

> If EOF is hit before n bytes are read, this will return the bytes read so far, along with io.EOF.

`Decode` only builds the YAML decoder when `consumeWhitespace` returns nil (`decoder.go:333`), so an early `io.EOF` means the YAML fallback never runs and the caller gets the JSON syntax error instead.

### What did you expect to happen?

A document should decode the same whether or not it happens to be followed by padding. `{a}` should decode to `map[a:<nil>]`, as `{a} ` already does.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

`staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/yaml/repro_test.go`:

```go
package yaml

import (
	"bytes"
	"testing"
)

func TestShortTrailingDocument(t *testing.T) {
	for _, in := range []string{"{a}", "{a} "} {
		var out interface{}
		d := NewYAMLOrJSONDecoder(bytes.NewReader([]byte(in)), 4096)
		if err := d.Decode(&out); err != nil {
			t.Errorf("Decode(%q) = %v, want it to decode as %q does", in, err, "{a} ")
		}
	}
}
```

```
go test -run TestShortTrailingDocument ./pkg/util/yaml/
```

### Anything else we need to know?

Scope: the decoder only takes this path when the stream begins with `{` (`IsJSONBuffer`); a stream that does not is given a YAML decoder directly in the constructor and is unaffected. So ordinary `apiVersion:`-style manifests do not hit this. It is reachable through `StreamVisitor.Visit` (`staging/src/k8s.io/cli-runtime/pkg/resource/visitor.go:590`) for a JSON-prefixed stream whose last document is under 4 bytes and is not valid JSON.

This is the same defect class as #142527 ("apimachinery yaml: keep a final line returned together with io.EOF"), in the same package: bytes returned alongside `io.EOF` are discarded by the caller. That change fixed one instance; this is another.

Happy to send a PR.

### Kubernetes version

<details>

```console
master at e7967bb9 (2026-10-03). Found by reading the code and reproduced with the unit test above, not against a running cluster.
```

</details>

### Cloud provider

N/A -- `k8s.io/apimachinery` library behaviour.

### OS version

N/A

N/A

N/A

title: HPA scales down above target when pods are unready
body:
Raising an issue that has been discussed for a while without a real solution.
Currently, for Object and External metrics with a `Value` target, the HPA computes:
```
desiredReplicas = ceil(usageRatio × readyPodCount)
```
 Pods could fail their readiness probes (due to overload or connection issue for example). As they do, `readyPodCount` falls, and so does `desiredReplicas`, even though the metric is above target.
In other words,  nothing prevents the `desiredReplicas` from dropping below the current replica count, so the HPA could scales the workload down while it is overloaded.

For example, with 10 current replicas and the metric at 2× target (`usageRatio = 2`):
| Ready pods | Proposal | Effect |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 10 | 20 | Scale up (correct) |
| 5 | 10 | No change, despite 2× load |
| **1** | **2** | **Scale down from 10 to 2** |

The scale-down stabilization window can delay this, but if the pods stay unready for longer than the window, the scale-down still happens. With a short window, it happens almost immediately.
Unready pods should be able to make a scale-up "smaller", but should never turn a scale-up into a scale-down.

This is easy to reproduce:
1. Deploy 10 pods with a readiness probe.
2. Deploy an HPA with one External `Value` metric with `target.value: 100`.
3. Have the external metrics server report 100 for that metric.
4. Make 9 of the 10 pods unready.
5. Set the metric to 200 (2× target).
6. The HPA scales the Deployment down to 2, with the event `New size: 2; reason: All metrics below target`.

My suggestion is to add a "direction guard" that checks whether the metric is above or lower the target:
- If the metric is **above** target, the HPA never proposes fewer replicas than it currently has. If there are too few ready pods to justify a scale-up, it holds at the current count instead of scaling down, and ideally reports that through an event or condition.
- If the metric is **below** target, the HPA never proposes more replicas than it currently has.
- Otherwise the calculation is unchanged.

For the same scenario (10 current replicas, metric at 2× target):
| Ready pods | Today | With guard |
|---|---|---|
| 10 | 20 | 20 |
| 5 | 10 | 10 |
| **1** | **2** | **10 (hold)** |

There were a few issues on that already and a few candidate solutions but none of them has ever reached consensus / implementation (#130130, #60886)
