title: [Scheduling] Add a Caching Mechanism for InterPodAffinity and PodTopologySpread Plugins
body:
## Motivation

In large clusters, `InterPodAffinity` and `PodTopologySpread` are among the most CPU-intensive scheduler plugins. Every scheduling cycle they walk the whole cluster to build the counts that `PreFilter`, `Filter`, `PreScore` and `Score` then read:

1. **InterPodAffinity PreFilter** — three walks: the existing pods' required anti-affinity terms matched against the incoming pod (over the snapshot's filtered anti-affinity node list), the incoming pod's own required terms matched against every pod of every node, and, with `InterPodAffinityHostnameFastPath`, a global count of the pods matching its host-scoped terms.
2. **InterPodAffinity PreScore** — for each node, every pod that carries affinity (or every pod at all, when the incoming pod has preferred terms of its own) matched against four sets of terms.
3. **PodTopologySpread PreScore** — for each node and each soft constraint, the node's pods matched against the constraint's selector and counted into the node's topology domain.

From one cycle to the next these walks are almost entirely redundant. Only the nodes that changed since the last cycle contribute something different; everything else is recomputed to the same number. The cost is O(nodes × pods) per cycle per pod shape, which is what a 5,000-node cluster pays on every pod of a rolling update, and what makes both plugins dominate the scheduler's CPU profile there.

### Goals

- Cut the per-cycle cost of the four walks to O(nodes changed) in the steady state, without changing any number they produce.
- Keep one source of truth. The counts a cycle decides on must be derived from the same snapshot that `Filter` and `Score` read in that cycle.
- Keep the community computation in the tree, both as the fallback and as the oracle the tests compare against.
- No locks, no background goroutines, no informer handlers, no lifecycle hooks.

### Non-Goals

- Caching results for `NodeAffinity` or any other plugin.
- Changing the scheduling algorithm, the scoring formulas or the filtering logic.
- Modifying the scheduler framework interfaces.
- Optimizing the scheduler's snapshot mechanism.
- Any user-facing API, configuration or metric.

## Proposal

A generic mechanism in `pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/nodememo`, plus three callers of it in `InterPodAffinity` and one in `PodTopologySpread`.

Each caller keeps one memoized **contribution per node**, validated with `framework.NodeInfo.GetGeneration()` and derived from the scheduling cycle snapshot:

```
  Cache.UpdateSnapshot            (first statement of every scheduling cycle)
            |
            v
  PreFilter / PreScore  ------>   NodeMemo[key(pod shape)]
            |                       part 1  serial    compare each node's generation, collect what moved
            |                       part 2  parallel  compute only those nodes' contributions
            |                       part 3  serial    fold the deltas into the aggregate
            v
  the counts / scores this cycle decides on
```

Because the aggregate is built from the snapshot that `Cache.UpdateSnapshot` just refreshed, and because every mutation that can change a node's contribution bumps that node's generation — `NodeInfo.update` for pods, `SetNode` and `RemoveNode` for the node itself, including the label changes that move it between topology domains — a count handed out by the memo always describes the cluster state this cycle is about to decide on. Staleness is not detected and then corrected; it is unrepresentable. This is the same invariant `Cache.UpdateSnapshot` itself relies on when it walks the cache's generation-ordered node list and stops at the first node that is not newer than the snapshot.

Generations come from one process-wide monotonic counter and one generation belongs to exactly one state of one node, so everything the memo decides follows from two rules:

- A stored contribution is reused only when the node still has the generation it was computed from. Equality, not "not older than", so a snapshot that goes back in time — which is what preemption's mutation session does, `StartMutations` handing out clones of every `NodeInfo` and `EndMutations` putting the originals back — is handled rather than misread.
- A node with no stored contribution and a generation no newer than the watermark contributed nothing when a previous pass looked at that very same state, so it contributes nothing now. Empty contributions are not stored, which is what keeps the memo sparse on a large cluster.

The second rule needs one more thing: the node must have been looked at. A caller may hand in a filtered list, and a node can drop out of such a list and come back later carrying the generation it left with, so the memo remembers the names of the nodes that left while contributing and recomputes them when they reappear instead of reading them as empty. That set is bounded; past the bound the memo forgets everything and the next pass rebuilds it, which is exact and costs one cold pass.

Only part 2 runs on the framework parallelizer, and each index writes its own result slot, so the memo needs no lock. Parts 1 and 3 run in the scheduling goroutine. A pass costs one generation read and one map lookup per node, plus the matching for the nodes that moved.

### Keying

One entry per pod shape, in a bounded LRU (10 by default), keyed by everything a per-node contribution depends on that no node generation can express: for `InterPodAffinity` the incoming pod's namespace and labels, the labels of that namespace, its required or preferred terms with their weights, and whether the incoming half runs at all; for `PodTopologySpread` the namespace, the constraints with their selectors, `requireAllTopologies`, and the pod's node selector, required node affinity and tolerations.

A key coarser than the inputs would have to be paired with an invalidation, and every invalidation costs a cold pass — which is dearer than the full computation the memo replaces, so two shapes alternating would leave the memo slower than having none. The incoming pod's own labels are deliberately *not* part of the `PodTopologySpread` key: nothing in its per-node computation reads them, the constraints were derived from them and are in the key themselves, so two workloads whose pods spread the same way share one entry. Selectors are fingerprinted through a helper that tells `labels.Nothing()` apart from `labels.Everything()`, which both render as the empty string.

### What the two paths share

Nothing is reimplemented. The per-node bodies are extracted from the existing code — `countExistingAntiAffinityOnNode`, `countIncomingOnNode`, `countMatchingHostScopedAffinityPodsOnNode`, `scoreNode`, `countNodePods` — and the full computation and the memo both call them, so the two cannot drift in what they count; only the traversal is incremental.

### Pod group cycles

A pod group cycle bypasses the memo and counts from the snapshot. It assumes every pod of the gang into one snapshot in place, `Snapshot.AssumePod` restores the old generation on purpose so that the snapshot stays consistent with the cache, and `Cache.UpdateSnapshot` runs once for the whole group. A generation that does not move while the node does is the one thing this design cannot detect. Counting from the snapshot is also what lets the later pods of a gang see the earlier ones.

### User Stories

**Large deployment rollout.** A 1,000-replica rolling update across a 5,000-node cluster with pod anti-affinity: every replica has the same shape, so all of them read one entry, and each cycle recomputes only the nodes that moved since the last one — in practice the node the previous replica was just assumed onto.

**High pod churn with topology spread.** A multi-tenant cluster with per-namespace spread constraints: the per-constraint counts are maintained as a delta over the nodes that changed, so a burst of pod creation costs one node recomputation per binding rather than a full cluster walk per pod.

**Topology-aware workload scheduling.** `TopologyAwareWorkloadScheduling` (KEP-5732, alpha in 1.36) picks a placement for a pod group by simulating the gang once per candidate placement, each simulation starting from a fresh cycle state, and a placement narrows the candidate nodes but not the counts: every pod of every simulation still walks the whole cluster in `PreFilter` and `PreScore`. A gang of M pods over N placements therefore pays M×N full recomputations of these counts inside one scheduling cycle. The memo is the mechanism that could take them away — a contribution depends only on the node's state and the pod's shape, so a cycle able to declare the nodes it assumed in place would build each cycle state as a delta over the one before it instead of from scratch, which is what makes the second pod of a gang and the second placement cheap. That is follow-up work: today a pod group cycle counts from the snapshot, because `Snapshot.AssumePod` deliberately keeps the old generation and a generation that does not move while the node does is the one thing this design cannot detect.

**Scale.** At 10,000 nodes the per-cycle cost of these plugins stops being O(nodes × pods) and becomes O(nodes) in generation comparisons plus O(changed nodes × pods) in matching.

### Risks and Mitigations

| Risk | Impact | Mitigation |
|------|--------|------------|
| A node mutated without its generation moving | High | The only path that does this is `Snapshot.AssumePod` / `ForgetPod`, which pin the generation on purpose so that the snapshot stays consistent with the cache; callers therefore bypass the memo in any pod group cycle, where those are the only in-place mutations. |
| Two pod shapes sharing one entry | High | The key holds every input the per-node computation reads, selectors fingerprinted so that `Nothing()` and `Everything()` differ. Tests pin each input, including the ones the fixtures do not vary. |
| Memory growth | Medium | Bounded LRU (10 shapes per memo) times one contribution per contributing node; empty contributions are not stored; topology values that reach zero are dropped. |
| Concurrency | Medium | Only the matching runs in parallel, one result slot per index; the two serial parts and all memo state live in the scheduling goroutine. No lock. |
| Cold pass dearer than the full computation | Low | Measured: 5–9% over it for `InterPodAffinity`, 19–32% for `PodTopologySpread`. A shape seen twice already pays for it; the LRU bound is what keeps a cluster of never-repeating shapes from thrashing. |
| The memo drifting from the community computation | Low | Both call the same per-node bodies; tests drive both through the real extension points over one snapshot and require identical results after every mutation. |

## Measured

Apple M4, `-benchtime=10x`, 20 pods per node plus the pods that put every node in the snapshot's filtered lists, one node moving between two passes — the shape of a rolling update:

| walk | 500 nodes | 2000 nodes | 5000 nodes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| InterPodAffinity PreFilter | 1.00ms → 32µs (31×) | 4.01ms → 100µs (40×) | 10.0ms → 267µs (37×) |
| InterPodAffinity PreScore | 258µs → 17µs (15×) | 1.66ms → 50µs (33×) | 4.05ms → 135µs (30×) |
| …host-scoped terms only | 247µs → 25µs (9.8×) | 1.11ms → 100µs (11×) | 2.93ms → 259µs (11×) |
| PodTopologySpread PreScore | 153µs → 44µs (3.5×) | 919µs → 151µs (6.1×) | 2.81ms → 390µs (7.2×) |

Allocations fall further than time does, because a steady pass allocates one result slot per recomputed node instead of one count list per node: `InterPodAffinity` `PreFilter` at 5000 nodes goes from 27.9MB and 65120 allocations per cycle to 12.5kB and 103, `PodTopologySpread` `PreScore` from 347kB and 5066 to 3.2kB and 62. Two workloads scheduled in turn — same namespace, same labels, different terms — measure 31× and 7.2×, so each keeps its own entry and there is no thrashing.

`PodTopologySpread`'s ratios are the smallest and that is the measurement rather than the mechanism: `initPreScoreState` is inside the timed loop because `PreScore` pays it every cycle whichever path it takes, and it walks the filtered nodes once per constraint, so it is a floor under both sides.

## Compatibility and testing

No feature gate and no API change. This is an internal recomputation of numbers the plugins already produce, and both paths are in the binary; a plugin that did not go through `New` has no memo and takes the full computation.

Tests drive a memoizing plugin and a copy of it with the memos taken out through the real `PreFilter` / `PreScore` / `Score` / `NormalizeScore` over one snapshot, and require identical results after every mutation: pods added, removed, terminating and matching nothing; a node moving between topology domains, losing its topology label, leaving the walked list and returning; a snapshot rolled back; the filtered nodes narrowed; the same shape in another namespace and in a namespace whose labels are identical to the first one's; a pod group cycle. Each walkthrough also runs with the parallel threshold at zero, and with `InterPodAffinityHostnameFastPath` / `EnableNodeInclusionPolicyInPodTopologySpread` on and off. Separate tests require that an unmoved snapshot recomputes nothing, that one moved node recomputes exactly one node, that only contributing nodes are stored, and that the keys separate every input.

title: PodGroup rejects system priority classes: spec.priority is capped at HighestUserDefinablePriority
body:
### What happened?

A PodGroup that references a built-in system PriorityClass is always rejected. Priority admission resolves `spec.priority` from the class ([admission.go#L203-L222](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0887d3330e9bb0489dac763160f2ca27702e7729/plugin/pkg/admission/priority/admission.go#L203-L222)), and the v1beta1 `PodGroupSpec.Priority` field caps it at `HighestUserDefinablePriority` ([types.go#L704](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0887d3330e9bb0489dac763160f2ca27702e7729/staging/src/k8s.io/api/scheduling/v1beta1/types.go#L704)). `system-cluster-critical` (2000000000) and `system-node-critical` (2000001000) are both above that cap:

```
PodGroup.scheduling.k8s.io "..." is invalid: spec.priority: Invalid value: 2000000000: must be less than or equal to 1000000000
```

With `WorkloadWithJob` enabled, any Job using a system priority class is stuck: the Workload is created, PodGroup creation fails, and no pods are ever created. The controller also emits no event when PodGroup creation fails ([job_scheduling_manager.go#L620-L623](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0887d3330e9bb0489dac763160f2ca27702e7729/pkg/controller/job/job_scheduling_manager.go#L620-L623)), so the error shows up only in the kube-controller-manager log.

### What did you expect to happen?

PodGroups (and Jobs) can use the system priority classes, just as Pods can. The user-defined cap should still apply to non-system classes.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Enable `GenericWorkload` and `WorkloadWithJob`, enable `scheduling.k8s.io/v1beta1`, then:

```yaml
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: PodGroup
metadata:
  name: pg
spec:
  priorityClassName: system-cluster-critical
  schedulingPolicy:
    basic: {}
```

The same request with a user-defined PriorityClass of value 1000000000 succeeds.

### Anything else we need to know?

The same `+k8s:maximum` tag is also on `PodGroupTemplate.Priority` ([L287](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0887d3330e9bb0489dac763160f2ca27702e7729/staging/src/k8s.io/api/scheduling/v1beta1/types.go#L287)) and `CompositePodGroupTemplate.Priority` ([L358](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0887d3330e9bb0489dac763160f2ca27702e7729/staging/src/k8s.io/api/scheduling/v1beta1/types.go#L358)), and on the matching v1alpha3 fields. Clamping the value in the controller won't work, because admission rejects a priority that doesn't match the class ([admission.go#L217-L219](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0887d3330e9bb0489dac763160f2ca27702e7729/plugin/pkg/admission/priority/admission.go#L217-L219)). The likely fix is to relax the API cap to match `PriorityClass` validation ([validation.go#L48-L55](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0887d3330e9bb0489dac763160f2ca27702e7729/pkg/apis/scheduling/validation/validation.go#L48-L55)) and also add a `FailedPodGroupCreate` event.

### Kubernetes version

master @ 0887d3330e9

N/A (kind)

title: PodGroup protection controller: inverted error check requeues successful keys forever and drops failed ones
body:
### What happened?

`processNextWorkItem` in `pkg/controller/scheduling/podgroupprotection/podgroup_protection_controller.go` has its error check inverted:

```go
err := processFunc(ctx, key)
if err != nil {
	queue.Forget(key)
	return true
}

queue.AddRateLimited(key)
utilruntime.HandleError(fmt.Errorf("%v %v failed with: %w", kind, key, err))
```

As a result:

1. **Successful syncs are requeued forever.** Every key processed without error is put back with `AddRateLimited` and logged at error level as `PodGroup <ns>/<name> failed with: %!w(<nil>)`. Because a missing object also returns `nil`, keys for PodGroups/CompositePodGroups that were already deleted keep cycling indefinitely (backoff caps at 1000s), and the rate limiter's per-item failure map grows with every PodGroup the controller has seen. `handlePodChange` enqueues the PodGroup whenever one of its pods reaches a terminal phase, so this hits every PodGroup with a completed pod, not only ones being deleted.

2. **Failed syncs are never retried.** If removing the finalizer fails (for example a 409 Conflict on the `Update`), the key is `Forget`-ed and dropped. A PodGroup or CompositePodGroup that is being deleted and has no remaining pods/children produces no further events, so it stays in `Terminating` until the next informer resync.


### What did you expect to happen?

Keys that sync successfully are forgotten; keys that fail are requeued with rate limiting, as in the standard controller pattern (and as before #141021).


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Unit-level reproduction against current master:

```go
q := workqueue.NewTypedRateLimitingQueue(workqueue.DefaultTypedControllerRateLimiter[string]())
q.Add("ns/pg")
processNextWorkItem(ctx, "PodGroup", q, func(context.Context, string) error { return nil })
// q.NumRequeues("ns/pg") == 1, and logs: "PodGroup ns/pg failed with: %!w(<nil>)"

q.Add("ns/pg2")
processNextWorkItem(ctx, "PodGroup", q, func(context.Context, string) error { return errors.New("conflict") })
// q.NumRequeues("ns/pg2") == 0 -> never retried
```

In a cluster: run kube-controller-manager with `--feature-gates=GenericWorkload=true`, create a PodGroup with a pod that completes, and watch the controller-manager repeatedly log `failed with: %!w(<nil>)` for that PodGroup.


### Anything else we need to know?

This regressed in #141021 (commit 86760556650) when `processNextWorkItem` was generalised to serve both the PodGroup and CompositePodGroup queues. The original implementation from #137641 used `if err == nil { Forget; return }`.

It is in v1.38.0-alpha.2 but not in any stable release yet.

The existing unit tests call `processPodGroup` / `processCompositePodGroup` directly and never exercise `processNextWorkItem`, which is why this was not caught. I'd like to send a fix that restores the check and adds a table test for `processNextWorkItem` covering both paths.

title: No e2e coverage for readiness probes during graceful pod termination
body:
### What happened?

#140881 was a total loss of exec readiness probing during the entire graceful termination window, shipped in v1.35.0 and caught by a user, not by CI. Nothing in the e2e suite asserts anything about probes after a pod's `deletionTimestamp` is set.

`test/e2e/common/node/container_probe.go` covers startup, ordering, timeouts, restart counts, and readiness before delete, but every readiness assertion happens while the pod is running normally. `test/e2e/node/pod_termination*.go` and the graceful-shutdown tests cover termination but assert on lifecycle, not readiness. So the probe path and the termination path are each well covered and the intersection is not covered at all.

The unit regression test added in #140882 (`TestProbeWorkersSurviveSyncContextCancellation`) pins the specific context plumbing, but it fakes the pod worker's cancellation. It would not catch a different regression that breaks probing during termination somewhere else in the stack, e.g. in `pod_workers.go` or in the CRI call path.

Filed as a follow-up to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140882#discussion_r3659065740, per @SergeyKanzhelev's request to keep the e2e work out of the backport-able patch.

### What did you expect to happen?

An e2e test that deletes a pod whose readiness probe starts failing on SIGTERM and asserts the pod's `Ready` condition flips to `False` well before the grace period ends.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

N/A, this is a coverage gap. To confirm it: revert #140882 on master and run `test/e2e/common/node` plus the node e2e probe suites. Everything passes.

### Anything else we need to know?

Sketch of the test, matching the manual repro in #140881:

- busybox container that touches `/tmp/ready`, traps `TERM` with `rm -f /tmp/ready; sleep 300`, then idles.
- exec readiness probe `cat /tmp/ready`, `periodSeconds: 1`, `failureThreshold: 1`.
- `terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60`.
- Wait for `Ready=True`, delete the pod, then assert `Ready=False` within ~10s, with the pod still in `Terminating`.

Two traps worth writing into the test as comments so the next person does not re-learn them:

1. Assert on the pod's `Ready` condition, not on EndpointSlice membership. The `deletionTimestamp` withdraws the endpoint immediately regardless of readiness, which masks the bug completely.
2. The grace period has to be long enough that the container is still alive when the assertion runs, otherwise the test passes for the wrong reason.

Coverage worth adding beyond the base case, in rough priority order:

1. exec readiness probe during termination (the actual regression).
2. HTTP readiness probe during termination. Not affected by #140881 because the HTTP prober does not take the probe context, but it is the same contract and nothing pins it.
3. Readiness recorded during termination is reflected in the pod status, so a preStop hook that intentionally fails readiness behaves as documented.

Home is probably `test/e2e/common/node/container_probe.go`. It should not be a `ConformanceIt` initially, since it asserts kubelet timing behavior rather than an API guarantee, but it is a reasonable promotion candidate later.

Happy to take this one. PR to follow once #140882 merges, so the test lands against the fixed behavior rather than a known-red baseline.

Related: #140881, #140882, #130487

<details>

```console
$ kubectl version
Client Version: v1.35.0
Server Version: v1.35.0
```

</details>

Gap exists on master and all supported branches.

title: Service creation cannot handle 100 QPS on 5,000-node clusters
body:
Service creation cannot sustain 100 QPS on a 5,000-node cluster, whereas other resources in the scale test (such as ConfigMaps and Secrets) handle 100 QPS without issues.

When we switched Service creation in the 5,000-node load test from sequential execution (~15.6 QPS) to 100 QPS, effective throughput dropped to ~5.5 Services/s and `POST services` requests timed out after 34s.

Looking at the ClusterIP allocation path, there appears to be lock contention serializing Service creation:
- Dynamic ClusterIP allocation holds a mutex across the entire allocation call, including the synchronous request that writes the `IPAddress` object to etcd.
- While that lock is held, updating the allocated and available IP gauges after each create or delete lists all existing `IPAddress` objects from the informer cache twice and parses every IP string to check subnet containment.

References:
- [5,000-node scale test run](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/pr-logs/pull/142740/pull-kubernetes-gce-master-scale-performance-5000/2107481865647558656)
- [ClusterIP allocation lock](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/registry/core/service/ipallocator/cidrallocator.go#L347-L371)
- [IPAddress creation and metric update](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/registry/core/service/ipallocator/ipallocator.go#L142-L169)

/cc @aojea @serathius

/sig scalability

title: [Flaking Test] [sig-testing] ci-kubernetes-e2e-gce-cos-alphafeatures-master kubetest.Timeout [gce-cos-alphafeatures-master, gce-cos-alphafeatures-1.37]
body:
### Which jobs are flaking?

sig-release-master-blocking#gce-cos-alphafeatures-master (`ci-kubernetes-e2e-gce-cos-alphafeatures-master`)
sig-release-1.37-blocking#gce-cos-alphafeatures-1.37 (`ci-kubernetes-e2e-gce-cos-alphafeatures-beta`, the fork of the same job)

Triage: https://storage.googleapis.com/k8s-triage/index.html?job=%5Eci-kubernetes-e2e-gce-cos-alphafeatures-master%24&test=%5ETimeout%24

Status 2026-10-08: non-blocking for v1.38.0-alpha.2 after kannon92's assessment in the SIG Node thread and Keisuke's confirmation; alpha.2 is released. The test-side change is #142402; its presubmits passed and it is waiting for review. The periodic job still needs checking after it merges. The flake still shows on alpha.2, with the same test-phase variance as before: two 2026-10-08 runs timed out (suite 91 Passed, 0 Failed, test phase about 105 and 109 minutes), while the runs that passed finished in 78 to 102 minutes. One of them, https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-gce-cos-alphafeatures-master/2108071920288141312, is a shape not seen before: the suite passed at minute 112 and teardown finished at minute 119.6, both inside the 120m budget, and only the fixed 30-second settle wait and the final resource listing ran the job about 7 seconds over. The issue stays open, still triage accepted and priority/critical-urgent. I hold the Release Signal follow-up for now.

Next step per upodroid is a test-side improvement by SIG Node. Release-impact assessment: @kannon92 stated in the SIG Node thread that this should not block v1.38.0-alpha.1 and that it should still be fixed for v1.38. No mitigation has been agreed yet.

Master count from the 2026-09-16 00:57 UTC run through the 2026-09-23 18:44 UTC run is 23 of 93 completed runs timed out (25%), 2 of the last 13. On 1.37 it is 1 of its last 4.

The recent failures share one pattern: suite passed, teardown interrupted by the timer. The numbers further down are the 2026-09-21 06:00 UTC snapshot.

### Which tests are flaking?

`kubetest.Timeout`. The e2e suite passes in all but one of the timed-out runs; in that one the timeout interrupted the suite.

### Since when has it been flaking?

Snapshot 2026-09-21 06:00 UTC. On master, 15 of the 61 runs since 2026-09-16 00:57 UTC hit the timeout: the first at 2026-09-17 13:04 UTC, the last two at 2026-09-21 00:16 UTC and 02:19 UTC, with passing runs in between. On the 1.37 fork, 7 of the 21 runs since 2026-09-16 01:00 UTC, the latest at 2026-09-20 13:03 UTC.

Examples:
- https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-gce-cos-alphafeatures-master/2101858636748820480 (2026-09-21 02:19 UTC)
- https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-gce-cos-alphafeatures-master/2101736329489420288 (2026-09-20 18:13 UTC)
- https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-gce-cos-alphafeatures-master/2101281830744363008 (2026-09-19 12:07 UTC)
- https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-gce-cos-alphafeatures-beta/2101658314709405696 (1.37, 2026-09-20 13:03 UTC)

### Testgrid link

https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-release-master-blocking#gce-cos-alphafeatures-master

### Reason for failure (if possible)

The job runs out of its kubetest budget, not out of tests. It passes `--timeout=120m` to kubetest, which covers cluster up, the tests and teardown. Up and teardown are steady at about 15 minutes together, which leaves roughly 105 minutes for the suite. In 14 of the 15 timed-out master runs the suite finished with `91 Passed | 0 Failed` after 105 to 112 minutes and the budget ran out in the teardown steps; in the other run ginkgo was interrupted at 113 minutes with one spec still running (`90 Passed | 1 Failed`).

The suite's runtime is not fixed. The same 91 specs took 76 minutes in a passing run on 2026-09-19 at 14:08 UTC (https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-gce-cos-alphafeatures-master/2101312282582585344) and 106 minutes in the timed-out run two hours earlier (https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-gce-cos-alphafeatures-master/2101281830744363008), on the same Kubernetes commit (`v1.38.0-alpha.0.948+96b5e4e3ae3f8d`) and the same COS image. So a code or image change alone does not explain the timeouts; whether something makes the resize path slower under some conditions is open. Across the 59 runs since 2026-09-16 the test phase ranged from 76 to 113 minutes; the 45 passing runs took 76 to 103 minutes with a median of 87, and passing and timed-out runs occur on the same commits.

Almost all of that variance sits in one feature. `[Feature:InPlacePodVerticalScaling]` is 63 of the 91 specs and took 57 minutes in the fast run and 86 in the slow one; the other 28 specs took 19 minutes in both. 62 of the 63 resize specs are slower in the slow run, by 20 seconds at the median and up to 83 seconds, with no single spec standing out, so the extra time is inside the resize specs themselves. What inside them is slower I have not established; the kubelet logs of both runs show no deferred or infeasible resizes.

This is the same shape as #141186 on `ci-kubernetes-e2e-gci-gce-alpha-features`, which runs almost the same focus. That was resolved by kubernetes/test-infra#37724: kubetest to `--timeout=180m`, the prow timeout to 3h20m, and the job moved to release-informing, on the basis that alpha-feature lanes do not fit the two-hour release-blocking budget. The note on that issue that the 1.37 blocking board shows the same thing (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/141186#issuecomment-5316283473) was not followed up for the sig-release jobs, which still have `--timeout=120m` and a 2h20m prow timeout in `config/jobs/kubernetes/sig-release/gce-cos-e2e-master.yaml` and `release-branch-jobs/1.37.yaml`.

### Anything else we need to know?

Update after upodroid's comment (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/142262#issuecomment-5759352510): the next step is on the test side. SIG Node is asked to look at reducing the resize specs' execution time or their run-to-run variance while keeping the coverage. Skipping the resize tests is not on the table, and a timeout increase or dashboard change is not agreed; it would come after that attempt, if at all.

Background for whoever picks it up: InPlacePodVerticalScaling is Stable since 1.35, and this lane is the only blocking coverage the 63 resize specs have. The sig-node node-e2e lanes skip `[Feature:InPlacePodVerticalScaling]` explicitly or do not focus on it; the node alpha-features lane (`ci-kubernetes-node-e2e-containerd-alpha-features`) ran 3 memory-backed-volume resize specs in its latest build, none of the 63. The job runs ginkgo with `--nodes=1`, and the presubmit alpha-features job sets `--ginkgo-parallel=1` explicitly, so I have not assumed parallelism is safe for these specs. The sibling job's uncensored timing distribution is in the comments.

Release impact should be reassessed for later cuts if it remains unresolved. FLAKY on the CI Signal board is a tracking category and says nothing about the cut.

title: kube-apiserver: watch termination can bypass shutdown rate limiting
body:
### What happened?

With `--shutdown-watch-termination-grace-period` > 0, the apiserver is supposed to rate limit the termination of active watches during graceful shutdown (#114925). Active watches can instead return before the rate limiter is installed, and those watches are closed without any pacing.

The cause is a race in `k8s.io/apiserver`'s graceful shutdown:

- Each watch calls [Done()](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.36.1/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/waitgroup/ratelimited_waitgroup.go#L70-L87) on a wait group when it ends. That call only blocks on the rate limiter if [Wait()](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.36.1/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/waitgroup/ratelimited_waitgroup.go#L95-L108) has already installed it. Any Done that runs earlier returns immediately, unpaced.
- Watch handlers and the drain coordinator wait on the same signal. Each watch handler watches [ShuttingDown()](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.36.1/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/lifecycle_signals.go#L153-L155) which is the NotAcceptingNewRequest signal. It [returns as soon as that fires](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.36.1/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/endpoints/handlers/watch.go#L299-L307).
- The drain coordinator listens for the same signal. It only calls `Wait()` after waking on [the same NotAcceptingNewRequest](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.36.1/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/genericapiserver.go#L676-L706). Nothing orders the coordinator against the watches.

Because these goroutines wake on the same signal, multiple watch handlers can reach `Done()` before the drain coordinator installs the limiter. One symptom is that `activeWatchesBefore` in the `[graceful-termination] active watch request(s) have drained` log is well below the number of watches that were open when shutdown began.

### What did you expect to happen?

With `--shutdown-watch-termination-grace-period` > 0, shutdown-triggered watch termination should use the configured rate limiting. The limiter should be initialized before active watch handlers are signaled to return, so scheduling between the watch handlers and the drain goroutine cannot bypass that pacing.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

The following unit test in k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server reproduces the missing ordering using the existing generic-apiserver test helpers. It does the following:

1. Start a `GenericAPIServer` with `ShutdownWatchTerminationGracePeriod > 0` (`newGenericAPIServer(t, ..., true)`).
2. Register a watch handler that blocks on `ServerShutdownSignalFrom(ctx).ShuttingDown()`. After the channel closes, probe `WatchRequestWaitGroup.Add(1)` and balance any successful call with `Add(-1)`. A successful `Add(1)` demonstrates that the handler observed shutdown before the wait group entered waiting mode.
3. Open 200 watches, then cancel the server context.

On master (`99a4ea72fe6`), the test failed in 50 of 50 runs (`-count=50`):

```
--- FAIL: TestGracefulTerminationWatchShutdownOrdering (1.19s)
    genericapiserver_graceful_termination_test.go:637: 1 of 200 watch handlers observed shutdown before the watch wait group entered waiting mode
--- FAIL: TestGracefulTerminationWatchShutdownOrdering (0.73s)
    genericapiserver_graceful_termination_test.go:637: 87 of 200 watch handlers observed shutdown before the watch wait group entered waiting mode
...
```

Across the 50 runs, between 1 and 197 of the 200 watch handlers observed shutdown before the watch wait group entered waiting mode. This demonstrates the missing ordering.

<details>
<summary>Test (applies to master as is)</summary>

```diff
diff --git a/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/genericapiserver_graceful_termination_test.go b/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/genericapiserver_graceful_termination_test.go
index 24d918ebf97..9f532990262 100644
--- a/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/genericapiserver_graceful_termination_test.go
+++ b/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/genericapiserver_graceful_termination_test.go
@@ -564,6 +564,80 @@ func TestGracefulTerminationWithKeepListeningDuringGracefulTerminationEnabled(t
 	}
 }
 
+// This test checks that the watch wait group has entered waiting mode
+// before active watch handlers observe the shutdown signal.
+func TestGracefulTerminationWatchShutdownOrdering(t *testing.T) {
+	s := newGenericAPIServer(t, &fakeAudit{}, true)
+	client := newClient(false)
+	doer := setupDoer(t, s.SecureServingInfo)
+
+	// the more watches, the more likely one of them wins the race
+	const n = 200
+	startedWG := sync.WaitGroup{}
+	startedWG.Add(n)
+	var lock sync.Mutex
+	var shutdownBeforeWait int
+	s.Handler.NonGoRestfulMux.Handle("/apis/watches.group/v1/namespaces/foo/bar", http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, req *http.Request) {
+		signals := apirequest.ServerShutdownSignalFrom(req.Context())
+		startedWG.Done()
+		if signals == nil {
+			w.WriteHeader(http.StatusInternalServerError)
+			return
+		}
+		<-signals.ShuttingDown()
+
+		// After observing shutdown, a positive Add should be rejected.
+		// Success means the watch wait group has not yet entered waiting mode.
+		if err := s.WatchRequestWaitGroup.Add(1); err == nil {
+			s.WatchRequestWaitGroup.Add(-1)
+			lock.Lock()
+			shutdownBeforeWait++
+			lock.Unlock()
+		}
+		w.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK)
+	}))
+
+	_, ctx := ktesting.NewTestContext(t)
+	stopCtx, stop := context.WithCancelCause(ctx)
+	defer stop(errors.New("test has completed"))
+	runCompletedCh := make(chan struct{})
+	go func() {
+		defer close(runCompletedCh)
+		if err := s.PrepareRun().RunWithContext(stopCtx); err != nil {
+			t.Errorf("unexpected error from RunWithContext: %v", err)
+		}
+	}()
+	waitForAPIServerStarted(t, doer)
+
+	resultCh := make(chan result, n)
+	for i := 0; i < n; i++ {
+		go func() {
+			resultCh <- doer.Do(client, func(httptrace.GotConnInfo) {}, "/apis/watches.group/v1/namespaces/foo/bar?watch=true", 0)
+		}()
+	}
+	startedCh := make(chan struct{})
+	go func() {
+		defer close(startedCh)
+		startedWG.Wait()
+	}()
+	waitForeverUntil(t, startedCh, "in-flight watch requests did not reach the server")
+
+	stop(errors.New("shutting down"))
+	for i := 0; i < n; i++ {
+		resultGot := <-resultCh
+		if err := assertResponseStatusCode(resultGot, http.StatusOK); err != nil {
+			t.Errorf("%s", err.Error())
+		}
+	}
+	waitForeverUntil(t, runCompletedCh, "the apiserver Run method did not return")
+
+	lock.Lock()
+	defer lock.Unlock()
+	if shutdownBeforeWait != 0 {
+		t.Errorf("%d of %d watch handlers observed shutdown before the watch wait group entered waiting mode", shutdownBeforeWait, n)
+	}
+}
+
 func TestMuxAndDiscoveryComplete(t *testing.T) {
 	// setup
 	testSignal1 := make(chan struct{})
```

Run with `go test ./staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server -run '^TestGracefulTerminationWatchShutdownOrdering$' -count=50`.

title: kube-proxy config validation reports internal field paths
body:
### What happened?

kube-proxy configuration validation reports error field paths using internal Go type and field names instead of the public `kubeproxy.config.k8s.io/v1alpha1` JSON/YAML field names.

For example, a config with invalid values for:

```yaml
apiVersion: kubeproxy.config.k8s.io/v1alpha1
kind: KubeProxyConfiguration
bindAddress: "10.10.12.11:2000"
healthzBindAddress: "0.0.0.0"
metricsBindAddress: "127.0.0.1"
iptables:
  masqueradeBit: 32
```

is reported by the validator as:

```text
KubeProxyConfiguration.KubeProxyIPTablesConfiguration.MasqueradeBit: Invalid value: 32: must be within the range [0, 31]
KubeProxyConfiguration.BindAddress: Invalid value: "10.10.12.11:2000": not a valid textual representation of an IP address
KubeProxyConfiguration.HealthzBindAddress: Invalid value: "0.0.0.0": must be IP:port
KubeProxyConfiguration.MetricsBindAddress: Invalid value: "127.0.0.1": must be IP:port
```

Those paths do not match the fields users put in kube-proxy config files:

```text
iptables.masqueradeBit
bindAddress
healthzBindAddress
metricsBindAddress
```

The same pattern appears in other kube-proxy validation paths, for example:

- `KubeProxyConfiguration.KubeProxyLinuxConfiguration.KubeProxyConntrackConfiguration.TCPEstablishedTimeout` instead of `conntrack.tcpEstablishedTimeout`
- `KubeProxyConfiguration.KubeProxyLinuxConfiguration.OOMScoreAdj` instead of `oomScoreAdj`
- `KubeProxyConfiguration.KubeProxyIPVSConfiguration.ExcludeCidrs` instead of `ipvs.excludeCIDRs`

The external field names are defined in `staging/src/k8s.io/kube-proxy/config/v1alpha1/types.go`, but `pkg/proxy/apis/config/validation/validation.go` constructs paths with internal names like:

```go
field.NewPath("KubeProxyConfiguration")
newPath.Child("BindAddress")
newPath.Child("KubeProxyIPTablesConfiguration")
fldPath.Child("MasqueradeBit")
```

The current unit tests also assert these internal paths, for example `pkg/proxy/apis/config/validation/validation_test.go` expects `BindAddress`, `KubeIPTablesConfiguration.MasqueradeBit`, and `KubeProxyLinuxConfiguration.KubeProxyConntrackConfiguration.*`.

### What did you expect to happen?

Validation errors for kube-proxy config should identify the public config file field paths, so users can copy the path back into their YAML/JSON and find the bad field directly.

Examples:

```text
iptables.masqueradeBit: Invalid value: 32: must be within the range [0, 31]
bindAddress: Invalid value: "10.10.12.11:2000": not a valid textual representation of an IP address
healthzBindAddress: Invalid value: "0.0.0.0": must be IP:port
metricsBindAddress: Invalid value: "127.0.0.1": must be IP:port
```

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

No cluster is required; this is pure kube-proxy config validation.

I reproduced on current master (`feb5375e`) by adding a temporary test under `pkg/proxy/apis/config/validation` that builds an otherwise valid `KubeProxyConfiguration`, sets invalid values for `BindAddress`, `HealthzBindAddress`, `MetricsBindAddress`, and `IPTables.MasqueradeBit`, then logs `Validate(config).ToAggregate()`.

The focused command:

```bash
mise exec go@1.27.0 -- go test ./pkg/proxy/apis/config/validation -run '^TestIssueReproKubeProxyConfigErrorPaths$' -count=1 -v
```

printed:

```text
[KubeProxyConfiguration.KubeProxyIPTablesConfiguration.MasqueradeBit: Invalid value: 32: must be within the range [0, 31], KubeProxyConfiguration.BindAddress: Invalid value: "10.10.12.11:2000": not a valid textual representation of an IP address, KubeProxyConfiguration.HealthzBindAddress: Invalid value: "0.0.0.0": must be IP:port, KubeProxyConfiguration.MetricsBindAddress: Invalid value: "127.0.0.1": must be IP:port]
```

The existing validation tests show the same paths without adding a repro test; for example:

```bash
mise exec go@1.27.0 -- go test ./pkg/proxy/apis/config/validation -run 'TestValidateKubeProxyConfiguration/invalid BindAddress|TestValidateKubeProxyIPTablesConfiguration|TestValidateKubeProxyIPVSConfiguration|TestValidateKubeProxyLinuxConfiguration' -count=1
```

passes today because the expected errors use the internal paths.

### Anything else we need to know?

This looks similar in shape to incorrect validation field path issues elsewhere: clients and users consume these paths as references to configuration fields, so they should match the external API surface rather than internal Go names.

Possible fix direction: make kube-proxy validation construct paths from the public v1alpha1 config layout (`bindAddress`, `iptables.masqueradeBit`, `ipvs.excludeCIDRs`, `conntrack.tcpEstablishedTimeout`, etc.) and update the validation tests accordingly.

Analysis prepared with AI assistance and verified with local code inspection plus the focused Go test above.

/kind bug
/sig network
/area kube-proxy

I'm starting to wonder whether the problem is getting worse again because we still don't catch new tests that use this anti-pattern (for example, https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/107763).

Is it time to start another spring clean which removes occurrences of this anti-pattern? Or perhaps add some mechanism that prevents it in new code?

I'm getting tired of seeing failures where the only output is
```
Expected error:

    }

not to have occurred
```

This is the result of
```
Expect(err).NotTo(HaveOccurred())
```

or more recently
```
ExpectNoError(err)
```

An explanation string would help, but even better solutions would be possible (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/106575).

title: [Scheduler] Redundant async preemption with already-deleted victim leaves preemptor stuck in unschedulable pool until 5-min flush
body:
## What happened?

With `SchedulerAsyncPreemption` enabled (default since 1.32), a preemptor pod can be parked in the unschedulable pod pool for the full `DefaultPodMaxInUnschedulablePodsDuration` (5m0s) even though its preemption completed successfully milliseconds after it started.

Race chain (log quotes are from a captured kube-scheduler v=5 log, v1.33.0):

1. Cycle N fails filter → PostFilter picks node X, starts async preemption, victim V is evicted successfully ("Async Preemption finished completely ... result=success").
2. The victim-deletion event immediately requeues the preemptor → cycle N+1 runs *before* the scheduler cache observes V is gone → filter fails again → PostFilter starts a **second, redundant async preemption** for the same node and victim.
3. The second preemption finds V already deleted ("Victim Pod is already deleted") → issues zero API calls → **no PodDelete event is emitted**.
4. The deletion event from the first preemption *did* fire, but arrived while cycle N+1 was in-flight; it was consumed during in-flight event evaluation ("Checking event for in-flight pod ... hint=1"), and the pod still landed in the unschedulable pool because cycle N+1's PostFilter had already synchronously re-inserted the preemptor's UID into the preempting set, latching DefaultPreemption's PreEnqueue pending gate: "waiting for the preemption for this pod to be finished".
5. The gate's release mechanism is a victim-deletion event (`DefaultPreemption.EventsToRegister` returns nil). None will ever come. In a quiet cluster (no unrelated pod/node churn), the pod sits untouched until the 5-minute flush:

```
21:50:55.472  "Async Preemption finished completely" result=success
<total silence for this pod>
21:55:55.337  next "Update event for unscheduled pod" (external teardown)
```

Related: #140082 / #140054 fixed the sibling variant where the victim is preempted in-memory (WaitingPod / PreBind cancel). That fix explicitly does NOT cover this variant: the "Victim Pod is already deleted" path in `PreemptPod` returns `preemptedInMemory=false, nil`, on the assumption that the earlier deletion event suffices. Under redundant preemption + in-flight event consumption, it does not.

## What did you expect to happen?

Once all async preemption work for a preemptor completes (successfully or as a no-op), the preemptor should be requeued promptly — the pending gate must not depend on a specific cluster event that a no-op preemption never produces.

## How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Conditions required: SchedulerAsyncPreemption on (default); a high-priority pod P that needs preemption of a lower-priority victim V on node X; P fails filter again in a retry cycle that runs after V's deletion is issued but before the scheduler cache reflects it (cache-lag window) → PostFilter re-runs and re-selects the same (node, victim) pair.

We hit this repeatedly in an integration environment: kwok-simulated cluster (kwok v0.7.0, k8s v1.33.0 binaries, --runtime=binary), a scheduler extender that keeps rejecting P's alternative nodes so P keeps retrying against node X, and a slow control plane (containerized CI on overlayfs) that widens the cache-lag window. When the race hits, the preemptor stalls for exactly 5 minutes (matches DefaultPodMaxInUnschedulablePodsDuration to the second).

A targeted scheduler integration test (test/integration/scheduler/preemption) that drives a redundant preemption against an already-deleted victim and asserts the preemptor leaves the unschedulable pool without waiting for the flush would reproduce it reliably.

## Anything else we need to know?

Suggested fix: in the async preemption goroutine (`prepareCandidateAsync`), treat the already-deleted last victim the same way #140054 treats the in-memory case — i.e. Activate the preemptor when no deletion event will be produced for the last victim. More generally, consider releasing the pending gate on async-preemption *completion* rather than on the eviction's observable side effect.

Why production clusters rarely notice: any unrelated cluster event whose QueueingHint returns Queue requeues the pod and the gate re-evaluates clean (the preemption finished long ago), so busy clusters self-heal in sub-second time. The full 5-minute stall only manifests in quiet clusters/queues — but the mechanism guarantee is still "worst case 5 min scheduling delay for a pod whose preemption already succeeded".

Evidence: full kube-scheduler v=5 log from the failing run is available on request (contains the complete cycle trace with in-flight event consumption).

## Kubernetes version

v1.33.0. Note #140054 (the partial sibling fix) is milestoned v1.37, so v1.33–v1.36 contain no fix at all for this family.

## Cloud provider

N/A — kwok-simulated cluster (sigs.k8s.io/kwok v0.7.0, binary runtime).

## OS version

Ubuntu (GitHub Actions runner), Docker container. Local macOS arm64 kwok runs do NOT reproduce (control plane too fast for the cache-lag window).

/sig scheduling

title: API Server Write Throughput: Reduce Write Allocations
body:
### What would you like to be added?

This issue tracks reducing write-path allocations from https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/142223.

Pod patch allocations were already reduced by ~35% in 1.37 (from ~152x down to ~98x), with ~70% of the remaining allocations on the write path (`handlers.PatchResource`) and ~30% in watch propagation. For 1.38, the goal is another ~50% reduction to reach the ~50x target.

![Pod Patch Allocation Factor Across 1.37 & 1.38](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/Jefftree/c38742b0d91e69f247b197ce1cebf501/raw/3cddeb56804ffe7b804cdff23c577fd1284e6599/retro_137_pod_write_chart.png)

Completed in 1.37:

- [x] https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/139350
- [x] https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/139826
- [x] https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/139851
- [x] https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/139856
- [x] https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/139974
- [x] https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140368
- [x] https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/141947
- [x] https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142227

Targeted for 1.38:

- ~5x (~1.6k allocs): Audit and remove avoidable `Pod` deep copies, equality allocations, and redundant conversions along the update pipeline
  - [x] https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142398
  - [ ] https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142743
- ~18x (~4.3k allocs): Reduce `managedFields` and SSA field-tracking allocations during writes (including reset fields)
  - [x] https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/structured-merge-diff/pull/351
  - [ ] https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142320
  - [ ] https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142427
- ~22x (~3.0k allocs): Reduce the unstructured conversion round-trip in Strategic Merge Patch (`ToUnstructured` / `FromUnstructuredWithValidation`)
  - [ ] https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142394

### Why is this needed?

`kube-apiserver` hits a Go runtime GC sweep ceiling around ~6 GB/s of allocations on large multicore nodes, limiting sustainable throughput when a 10 KB Pod patch allocates ~1 MB.

Write-path breakdown for a 10 KB Pod (`BenchmarkPatchPod` in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/142227):

| Component | Factor | Bytes / op | Notes |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Strategic Merge Patch | ~25x | ~256 KB | Unstructured map round-trip (`ToUnstructured` -> `SMP` -> `FromUnstructuredWithValidation`) |
| `managedFields` / SSA | ~20x | ~204 KB | `FieldManager.Update` and `ValidateManagedFields` |
| `Pod` copies & conversion | ~17x | ~170 KB | ~4-5 full `Pod` deep copies (18.8 KB each) and version conversions |
| Request, admission & framing | ~11x | ~120 KB | Handler, admission, and HTTP framing overhead |
| Validation | ~7x | ~76 KB | `ValidatePodUpdate` |
| Protobuf serialization | ~7x | ~68 KB | Storage and response serialization |
| Total write path | ~87x | ~894 KB | `15,133 allocs/op` (`~78x` / `796 KB` / `13,751 allocs/op` on `PatchPodStatus`) |

title: Support the HTTP QUERY method (RFC 10008) in API server proxy subresources
body:
/sig api-machinery
/kind feature

### What would you like to be added?

Add `QUERY` to the HTTP methods accepted by the API server proxy
subresources (at minimum services, ideally pods and nodes too):

- /api/v1/namespaces/{ns}/services/{name}/proxy/{path}
- /api/v1/namespaces/{ns}/pods/{name}/proxy/{path}
- /api/v1/nodes/{name}/proxy/{path}

`kubectl proxy` forwards to these endpoints, so it would gain the
support without separate changes.

### Why is this needed?

QUERY is now a standards-track HTTP method, defined in RFC 10008
(https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc10008). It is a safe, idempotent
request method that carries content, so clients can send complex
queries without putting them in the URL and without using POST. Because
it is safe and idempotent, caches and clients can safely retry it.

The proxy subresources only forward an allowlist of methods. On master,
`proxyMethods` in pkg/registry/core/service/proxy.go is:

    []string{"GET", "POST", "PUT", "PATCH", "DELETE", "HEAD", "OPTIONS"}

`ConnectMethods()` returns this list, so a QUERY request through the
proxy is expected to be rejected with 405 Method Not Allowed instead of
reaching the backend. (I have not yet confirmed this on a running
cluster.) As a result, backends that implement QUERY (search and
query-style APIs) cannot be reached through `kubectl proxy` or the API
server proxy.

I searched kubernetes/kubernetes and the kubernetes org for existing
issues about QUERY or the IETF draft (safe-method-w-body) and found
none.

### Possible approach

Add "QUERY" to the proxy method lists for the affected subresources.
Open questions for maintainers:
- Should this apply to services only, or to pods and nodes as well?
- Does the API server's request handling, authorization (verb mapping),
  or audit logging need changes for a new method?

### Workarounds today

`kubectl port-forward`, or fronting the service with a gateway or
ingress that passes arbitrary methods.

title: [Feature][scheduler] Asynchronously or concurrently update (Composite)PodGroup status conditions to avoid scheduling cycle head-of-line blocking
body:
/sig scheduling
/area scheduler
/kind feature
### Description
In https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140670, status condition updates for `PodGroup` and `CompositePodGroup` were integrated into the scheduler pipeline.
Currently, in `submitPodGroupAlgorithmResult` (`pkg/scheduler/schedule_one_podgroup.go`), status updates for every group within a hierarchy are performed sequentially and synchronously on the main scheduling goroutine:
```go
for _, podGroupResult := range podGroupResults {
    pgi := podGroupResult.podGroupInfo
    if pgi.CompositePodGroup != nil {
        sched.submitCompositePodGroupResult(ctx, podGroupResult)
        continue
    }
    queuedPodInfos := rootPodGroupInfo.QueuedPodInfos[pgi.GetKey()]
    sched.submitPodGroupResult(ctx, schedFwk, podGroupState, queuedPodInfos, podGroupResult)
}
```
Each call to `submitCompositePodGroupResult` / `submitPodGroupResult` issues an individual, synchronous status patch request to the API server (`util.PatchPodGroupStatus` / `util.PatchCompositePodGroupStatus`).
### Why this is a problem
For larger or deeper hierarchies containing multiple intermediate composite groups and leaf pod groups, issuing sequential synchronous HTTP patch calls directly on the scheduling thread:
- Multiplies scheduling cycle latency linearly by the number of groups in the subtree.
- Contributes to head-of-line (HoL) blocking in the active scheduling queue, as the scheduler cannot pick up the next queued workload until all status updates complete.
### Potential Mitigations to Discuss
- **Asynchronous dispatch**: Offload status patching to background goroutines (similar to `sched.runBindingCycle`) or a dedicated worker queue so the main scheduling goroutine can immediately proceed to the next cycle.
- **Concurrent patching**: If status updates must be bounded or completed within the cycle, patch group statuses concurrently (e.g., using an `errgroup` or bounded worker pool) rather than strictly sequentially.

title: tests: avoid generic poll functions
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Tests that use `wait.PollImmediate` (directly or indirectly, as in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ed07515ee012207e79816b4641ad5d3be238468b/test/e2e/framework/pod/wait.go#L386-L426) with a custom test function fail poorly when polling times out. Example:

```
/go/src/k8s.io/kubernetes/_output/dockerized/go/src/k8s.io/kubernetes/test/e2e/storage/pvc_protection.go:72
Nov 13 14:20:10.683: While creating pod that uses the PVC or waiting for the Pod to become Running
Unexpected error:
    <*errors.errorString | 0xc003d86070>: {
        s: "pod \"pvc-tester-w2jjx\" is not Running: timed out waiting for the condition",
    }
    pod "pvc-tester-w2jjx" is not Running: timed out waiting for the condition
occurred
/go/src/k8s.io/kubernetes/_output/dockerized/go/src/k8s.io/kubernetes/test/e2e/storage/pvc_protection.go:96
```

This is actually one of the better examples. In other cases the only failure message is "timed out waiting for the condition" without any indication what the condition was expected to be. Even in this example it is not clear what the state of the pod was in the end. Were there some events for the pod? What's its status?

Example from 2025, after conversion to `wait.PollUntilContextTimeout`:
```
[FAILED] client rate limiter Wait returned an error: context deadline exceeded
In [It] at: k8s.io/kubernetes/test/e2e/apimachinery/resource_quota.go:544
```

Logging inside the callback is necessary to provide developers some feedback while waiting for a test to finish. But when run inside the CI, that log output becomes spammy (e.g. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/136260). It therefore has to be short, which makes it less useful for interactive use.

A better way to write such tests is with `gomega.Eventually` and a custom matcher. `Eventually` handles the polling. In case of a failure, the matcher is called to produce a failure report which then can include arbitrary additional information that currently developers have to start hunting for in log files, if they can be found there at all. No log output is produced while polling. Instead, sending `SIGUSR1` to a running test binary or command line flags produce a progress report with detailed information about where and why a test is stuck.

Metrics testing is another example where some data is checked against certain expectations. Because the data is never logged, it is impossible to tell after a failure what went wrong.

**Update**: originally this issue was about E2E tests, but it also applies to integration and unit tests. With ktesting available as k8s.io/ktesting, it can be used everywhere and with [TContext.Eventually](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/48967d98cc29114b76c1d44158b66f62997cf194/staging/src/k8s.io/ktesting/assert.go#L261-L333) and friends offers a simple way of polling with gomega.


### Why is this needed?

Easier debugging after an test failure.

title: preStop sleep continues after PID 1 exits
body:
### What happened?

I've configured the podSpec of a Job to include a preStop sleep lifecycle hook. If the Pod is asked to terminate before it completes, the preStop sleep begins and runs for its full duration - even if the Pod completes its processing and PID 1 exits before the preStop sleep is complete. The Pod remains in "Terminating" and the Job remains in "Running" state until the preStop sleep finishes, which delays the completion of the Job.

### What did you expect to happen?

I expect the preStop sleep to end when PID 1 in the Pod exits. The Job should be marked as complete at that time and the Pod should finish terminating. This is the behavior when a preStop exec is used to run the sleep command in the container's shell.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Define a Job with a preStop sleep lifecycle hook:

```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: sleep-job
spec:
  podReplacementPolicy: Failed
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - command:
          - /bin/sleep
          - "60"
          image: busybox:latest
          name: sleep-container
          lifecycle:
            preStop:
              sleep:
                seconds: 120
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 120
      restartPolicy: Never
```

Apply the manifest and then delete the resulting Pod. Observe that the Pod is now in "Terminating" state. The preStop sleep will have begun.

```console
wedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl apply -f sleep-job.yaml 
job.batch/sleep-job created
wedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl get jobs,pods
NAME                  STATUS    COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
job.batch/sleep-job   Running   0/1           6s         6s

NAME                  READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
pod/sleep-job-qh2qk   1/1     Running   0          6s
wedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl delete pods sleep-job-qh2qk
pod "sleep-job-qh2qk" deleted
^Cwedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl get jobs,pods
NAME                  STATUS    COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
job.batch/sleep-job   Running   0/1           24s        24s

NAME                  READY   STATUS        RESTARTS   AGE
pod/sleep-job-qh2qk   1/1     Terminating   0          24s
```

After 60 seconds the Pod should complete but instead it remains in Terminating state and the Job shows 0 completions. Only after 2 minutes has elapsed (from the time the `delete` command was issued) does the Pod finish terminating and the Job shows a completion.

```console
wedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl get jobs,pods
NAME                  STATUS    COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
job.batch/sleep-job   Running   0/1           59s        59s

NAME                  READY   STATUS        RESTARTS   AGE
pod/sleep-job-qh2qk   1/1     Terminating   0          59s
wedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl get jobs,pods
NAME                  STATUS    COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
job.batch/sleep-job   Running   0/1           69s        69s

NAME                  READY   STATUS        RESTARTS   AGE
pod/sleep-job-qh2qk   1/1     Terminating   0          69s
wedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl get jobs,pods
NAME                  STATUS    COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
job.batch/sleep-job   Running   0/1           2m19s      2m19s

NAME                  READY   STATUS        RESTARTS   AGE
pod/sleep-job-qh2qk   1/1     Terminating   0          2m19s
wedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl get jobs,pods
NAME                  STATUS     COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
job.batch/sleep-job   Complete   1/1           2m21s      2m22s
```


### Anything else we need to know?

This kind of configuration is useful to ensure that batch jobs run to completion even if they are asked to terminate for whatever reason (maintenance, preemption, autoscaler consolidation, etc.). The fact that the Job takes longer to complete when the Pod is asked to terminate is problematic when timely completion of the Job is desired. Imagine that the Job takes an hour instead of a minute and so the prestop sleep is set to 3600. Then imagine that the Pod is asked to terminate at minute 59. The duration of the Job will now be 119 minutes instead of 60.

Using a preStop exec to run /bin/sleep produces the expected behavior where the Pod finishes terminating and the Job shows as complete when PID 1 in the container exits. Of course this won't work in a shell-less container which AFAIK is the reason the preStop sleep was introduced.

```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: exec-job
spec:
  podReplacementPolicy: Failed
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - command:
          - /bin/sleep
          - "60"
          image: busybox:latest
          name: exec-container
          lifecycle:
            preStop:
              exec:
                command: ["/bin/sleep", "120"]
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 120
      restartPolicy: Never
```

```console
wedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl apply -f exec-job.yaml 
job.batch/exec-job created
wedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl get jobs,pods
NAME                 STATUS    COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
job.batch/exec-job   Running   0/1           4s         4s

NAME                 READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
pod/exec-job-k62r4   1/1     Running   0          4s
wedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl delete pods exec-job-k62r4
pod "exec-job-k62r4" deleted
^Cwedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl get jobs,pods
NAME                 STATUS    COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
job.batch/exec-job   Running   0/1           23s        23s

NAME                 READY   STATUS        RESTARTS   AGE
pod/exec-job-k62r4   1/1     Terminating   0          23s
wedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl get jobs,pods
NAME                 STATUS    COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
job.batch/exec-job   Running   0/1           55s        55s

NAME                 READY   STATUS        RESTARTS   AGE
pod/exec-job-k62r4   1/1     Terminating   0          55s
wedge@pop-os:~/job-sleep$ kubectl get jobs,pods
NAME                 STATUS    COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
job.batch/exec-job   Running   0/1           61s        61s

NAME                 READY   STATUS        RESTARTS   AGE
pod/exec-job-k62r4   1/1     Terminating   0          61s

NAME                 STATUS     COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
```

title: Kubelet rejects pod with 'TaintToleration' due to stale informer cache
body:
### What happened? This seems very similar to #133997. When running a Karpenter node on AKS, we occasionally observe the following sequence: 1. Karpenter allocates a node, which initially comes up with the `karpenter.sh/unregistered:NoExecute` taint. 2. Karpenter then removes this taint from the node once certain conditions are met. 3. A pod is scheduled by the scheduler on this node very shortly after the taint has been removed 4. Kubelet rejects the pod because it believes the pod does not tolerate the taint the node had - but the node in fact no longer has this taint, just kubelet informer has not updated yet. Here's a sample event sequence with timestamps from kubeaudit: **Date:** `2026-10-01` **Objects:** `pod` = `redacted-pod-name-1234567890`, `node` = `aks-batch-fc7hd` | Time | Request | Object | Agent | Phase / result | Taints | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | 09:01:51.8626126 | patch pods/status | pod | Scheduler | Pending | — | | 09:01:52.1881284 | create nodes | node | Kubelet | — | `app=batch:NoSchedule`
`karpenter.sh/unregistered:NoExecute`
`node.cloudprovider.kubernetes.io/uninitialized=true:NoSchedule`
`node.kubernetes.io/not-ready:NoSchedule` | | 09:01:52.2059619 | patch nodes/status | node | Kubelet | — | — | | 09:01:52.2566700 | patch nodes | node | TTL controller | — | `app=batch:NoSchedule`
